sense: severely plain or strict, without comfort
definition: Severely plain and strict, with no comfort, luxury or decoration.
nuance: Austere describes places, styles, lives and people that are plain, strict and without comfort. It can be admiring (an austere, elegant design) or critical (a cold, austere manner). In economics it is linked to austerity, meaning deep cuts in public spending.

examples.text: The monks' cells were austere: a narrow bed, a wooden chair and nothing at all on the walls.
Modernist architects favoured austere forms, rejecting the decoration that Victorian builders loved.
The council has set an austere budget, freezing spending on everything except schools.
My gran's house was so austere; she thought cushions were a waste of money.
Applicants should expect austere living conditions at the research station, with shared rooms and no internet.
Her father's austere face softened only when he spoke about the sea.

cloze.text: The headmaster was ___ in every way: stern and unsmiling, and living in bare rooms without a single comfort.
He lived an ___ life, giving away most of his money and eating only the plainest food.
Unlike the richly decorated churches of Rome, the chapel has an ___ beauty: bare stone, plain glass and not a single ornament.

misuse.text: The party was austere, with loud music, fancy food and decorations everywhere.
misuse.why: Austere means plain and without luxury, the opposite of a lavish party.

misuse.text: The government will austere public spending next year.
misuse.why: Austere is an adjective, not a verb; say the government will cut spending or impose austerity.

phrases: ...in the austere years after the war

synonyms.vs: Stark is blunter and often bleak or harsh; austere can suggest deliberate, dignified simplicity.
Spartan describes basic, uncomfortable living conditions; austere also covers style, manner and moral strictness.
Severe is broader, used for weather, illness and punishment; austere is mainly about plainness and self-denial.

origin: From Latin austerus, from Greek austeros, 'harsh' or 'severe'.

sense: made up of separate episodes or events
definition: Made up of separate events or scenes that are only loosely linked, rather than one continuous whole.
nuance: Episodic describes novels, films, histories and memories built from separate scenes or events rather than one continuous story; calling a novel episodic is often a mild criticism of a weak plot. In psychology, episodic memory is memory of specific personal events, such as a birthday. It can also mean happening now and then (episodic pain), but that is a different sense.

examples.text: The novel is episodic: each chapter tells a separate adventure, with almost nothing linking one to the next.
Episodic memory allows us to recall specific events, such as our first day at school.
Reviewers found the new series too episodic, a string of stand-alone stories with no real plot connecting them.
I prefer episodic shows, where you can start anywhere without needing to know what came before.
The report takes an episodic approach, examining six separate incidents rather than tracing one continuous history.
Her memories of that summer were episodic: bright single scenes, with nothing at all in between.

cloze.text: Like a TV series of stand-alone stories, the novel is ___: each chapter is a self-contained adventure with the same hero.
Psychologists contrast semantic memory, for general facts, with ___ memory, for specific events you lived through at a particular time and place.
The biography is ___ rather than continuous, built from separate scenes of the writer's life with little to link them.

misuse.text: The film is episodic, one single unbroken shot that follows the hero through a continuous story.
misuse.why: Episodic means made of separate scenes or events, so it cannot describe one continuous, unbroken story.

misuse.text: Each episodic of the series lasts about forty minutes.
misuse.why: Episodic is an adjective; one part of a series is an 'episode'.

phrases: ...is largely episodic, moving from one incident to the next.

synonyms.vs: Fragmented suggests broken pieces and is clearly critical; episodic describes separate, complete parts and can be neutral.
Disjointed means badly connected and is always a criticism; episodic simply means built from separate parts.
Picaresque describes episodic novels about the adventures of a rogue or wanderer; episodic is the general term.

origin: From episode, from Greek epeisodion, originally a scene that came between the choral songs in a Greek tragedy.

definition: Wicked, dishonest or criminal, especially of plans or activities.
nuance: Nefarious is used about schemes, purposes and activities rather than ordinary bad behaviour. It sounds dramatic, so writers often use it with a touch of humour or irony. In serious writing it suits deliberate wrongdoing such as fraud or spying.

examples.text: The gang used the empty warehouse for nefarious purposes, including hiding stolen cars.
Historians still debate whether the spy ring's activities were truly nefarious or simply exaggerated by the press.
My cat is clearly planning something nefarious; she's been staring at the fish tank all morning.
The villain explained his nefarious plan in great detail, giving the hero time to escape.
Staff must report suspicious emails, as these may be sent for nefarious ends such as stealing data.
Police say the leaked passwords could be bought by anyone with nefarious intentions.

cloze.text: The hackers set up the fake charity website for ___ purposes: to steal donors' bank details and sell them to criminals.
In the novel, the kindly uncle is really a villain, and his ___ plot to steal his niece's fortune is uncovered only in the final chapter.
Cheap drones help farmers, but criminals have found more ___ uses for them, such as smuggling drugs into prisons.

misuse.text: The charity's nefarious work feeds thousands of families every winter.
misuse.why: Nefarious means wicked, so it cannot describe helpful charity work.

misuse.text: I made a nefarious mistake when I forgot my keys this morning.
misuse.why: Nefarious describes deliberate wickedness, not a harmless accident.

phrases: ...could be exploited by those with nefarious intentions.

synonyms.vs: Wicked is everyday and broad; nefarious is formal and mainly describes schemes and criminal activity.
Villainous suggests a story villain and can be theatrical; nefarious is used more for real plans and activities.
Sinister means seeming threatening or evil; nefarious means actually wicked or criminal.

roots.meaning: a crime, something against divine law (Latin)

origin: From Latin nefarius, from nefas, 'a wrong or crime', literally something against divine law.

definition: More than is needed or wanted, and so unnecessary.
nuance: Superfluous is formal and common in editing and feedback: superfluous words, detail or decoration. It is mildly critical, suggesting something could be removed with no loss. People also feel superfluous when they are not needed in a situation.

examples.text: Cut any superfluous words from your essay; if a sentence works without them, they are not needed.
Critics say the new road signs are superfluous, since almost every driver already uses satnav.
I felt a bit superfluous at the meeting, since they'd already made all the decisions.
The final report removes superfluous detail so that readers can focus on the key findings.
Her umbrella seemed superfluous by then; she was already soaked to the skin.
Ockham's razor advises against superfluous assumptions when a simpler explanation will do.

cloze.text: Like water spilling over the top of a full glass, ___ words go beyond what a sentence needs, so good editors cut them.
Adding 'very' to 'enormous' is a ___ touch, since the word is already as big as it can get.
With twelve speeches already planned, a thirteenth seemed ___, more than anyone in the hall needed or wanted.

misuse.text: Water is superfluous to human life; we cannot survive without it.
misuse.why: Superfluous means more than is needed, the opposite of essential.

misuse.text: She gave a superfluous performance and won every award going.
misuse.why: Superfluous means unnecessary, not superb or outstanding.

synonyms.vs: Redundant often means no longer needed, and in Britain can mean losing your job; superfluous simply means extra.
Unnecessary is everyday and neutral; superfluous is formal and suggests excess.
Excessive means too much of something; superfluous means a thing that is not needed at all.

confusables.note: Superficial means on the surface only, or shallow.

origin: From Latin superfluus, 'overflowing', from super, 'over', and fluere, 'to flow'.

definition: Happening, moving or existing at exactly the same time or rate.
nuance: Synchronous is technical and formal, common in science, technology and history. In online learning, synchronous classes happen live, while asynchronous ones are done at your own pace. It describes events, processes and movements rather than people.

examples.text: The course has synchronous lessons, when everyone logs in at the same time, and recorded ones you watch later.
The study found that the rise in sea temperature was synchronous with the decline of the coral reefs.
Fireflies in some forests flash in synchronous waves, lighting up whole valleys at once.
Synchronous communication, such as a phone call, requires both people to be available at once.
Is the seminar synchronous, or can I just watch the recording later?
The rowers' synchronous strokes carried the boat smoothly across the still lake.

cloze.text: Unlike recorded lectures, ___ classes take place live, with everyone online at the same moment.
The satellite's orbit is ___ with the Earth's spin: it circles at exactly the same rate as the planet turns, so it seems to hang over one spot.
Unlike email, a video call is ___ communication: both people must take part in real time, at the same moment.

misuse.text: The synchronous lecture can be watched at any time that suits you.
misuse.why: Synchronous means happening live at the same time for everyone; a lecture watched whenever you like is asynchronous.

misuse.text: The two sisters are very synchronous and always agree with each other.
misuse.why: Synchronous describes timing, not people getting on; say they are close or like-minded.

synonyms.vs: Simultaneous means happening at the same moment; synchronous also suggests a shared rhythm or coordinated timing.
Concurrent means happening during the same period, often loosely; synchronous suggests closer, more exact timing.
Contemporaneous means existing in the same historical period; synchronous is more exact and often technical.

origin: From Greek synchronos, from syn, 'together', and chronos, 'time'.

definition: To support or strengthen an argument, position or system, often with extra evidence or help.
nuance: Buttress is a formal verb borrowed from architecture, where a buttress is a stone support built against a wall. It is common in academic writing for evidence that strengthens a claim, and in news for money or measures that prop up an economy or institution. It suggests solid, added support.

examples.text: She buttressed her argument with data from three independent surveys, making it very hard to dismiss.
The central bank cut interest rates to buttress the struggling economy.
The new evidence buttresses the committee's view that the scheme has worked.
You'll need to buttress that claim with more than just a feeling.
She buttressed her story with so many small, convincing details that no one thought to doubt it.
Strong essays make a claim before buttressing it with evidence and careful analysis.

cloze.text: Like the stone supports of a cathedral wall, the case studies ___ the book's central claim.
Her shaky theory needed propping up, and fresh data from the trial ___ it, much as a mason shores up a leaning wall.
The minister is ___ his position by placing loyal allies on every key committee.

misuse.text: His weak evidence buttressed the argument so badly that the jury rejected it.
misuse.why: To buttress is to strengthen; weak evidence that damages an argument undermines it.

misuse.text: She buttressed against the door to keep the wind out.
misuse.why: Buttress means to strengthen something and needs an object; for pushing your body against a door, say 'braced herself'.

synonyms.vs: Reinforce is broader and more common; buttress sounds more formal and suggests support added from outside.
Bolster is often used for confidence, morale or numbers; buttress more often for arguments and structures.
Underpin means to form the base something rests on; buttress means to add support to something already standing.

origin: First a stone support built against a wall, from Old French bouter, 'to push'.

sense: come together to form one whole
definition: To come together and form a single group, mass or idea.
nuance: Coalesce is formal and usually describes something gradual: groups forming an alliance, scattered thoughts forming a plan, droplets forming a stream. Things coalesce by themselves, often 'into' or 'around' something. It suggests natural merging rather than forced combination.

examples.text: The small local groups coalesced into a single national movement within a year.
Over millions of years, dust and gas coalesced to form the planets.
My ideas for the essay finally coalesced at about two in the morning.
Support is coalescing around a compromise version of the proposal.
Every evening the mist coalesces over the marsh, thick enough to hide the path.
Raindrops grow as tiny droplets collide and coalesce inside the cloud.

cloze.text: In physics, two drops of oil that touch will ___, growing together into one larger drop.
Over the summer, a loose set of ideas slowly ___ into a clear plan for the business.
Scattered rebel groups began ___ around a single leader, gradually forming one united army.

misuse.text: The band coalesced after a bitter argument and never played together again.
misuse.why: Coalesce means come together into one; a band breaking up is the opposite.

misuse.text: The teacher coalesced the students into the hall for assembly.
misuse.why: Coalesce describes things merging by themselves, not someone moving people; say 'gathered' or 'led'.

synonyms.vs: Merge is everyday and can be deliberate, as when companies merge; coalesce suggests gradual, natural joining.
Unite stresses common purpose, usually of people; coalesce can also describe things, ideas or substances.
Fuse suggests joining completely, often by heat; coalesce stresses many parts gradually forming one.

origin: From Latin coalescere, 'to grow together', from co-, 'together', and alescere, 'to grow'.

sense: speak or write about someone very unfairly
definition: To say or write very harsh and unfair things about someone, damaging their reputation.
nuance: Vilify is strongly negative and suggests the attack is unfair or exaggerated. It is often used of the press, campaigns and crowds that turn a person or group into a villain. It is common in the passive: 'was vilified by'.

examples.text: The referee was vilified in the papers after the final, even though replays showed he was right.
Early critics vilified the Impressionists, calling their paintings unfinished and ugly.
It's not fair to vilify her online just because she left the show.
The code of conduct bans any post that vilifies a person because of their background.
For years the villagers vilified the old woman as a witch, though she had only ever helped them.
Wartime propaganda often works by vilifying the enemy, presenting them as cruel and inhuman.

cloze.text: The tabloids ___ the singer for months, printing cruel and false stories about her private life.
It is easy to ___ a whole group of people as villains instead of trying to understand them.
Rather than ___ their opponents with insults, the candidates agreed to debate the facts calmly.

misuse.text: The newspaper vilified the nurse, praising her bravery during the floods.
misuse.why: To vilify is to attack someone's reputation, not to praise them.

misuse.text: He vilified the cake by dropping it on the kitchen floor.
misuse.why: Vilify is about speaking badly of people, not damaging objects; say he ruined the cake.

phrases: Rather than vilifying..., this essay seeks to understand...

synonyms.vs: Criticise can be fair and balanced; vilify means attacking someone harshly and usually unfairly.
Demonise means portraying someone as evil or dangerous; vilify focuses on abusive, damaging words.
Malign stresses false or unfair claims, often quietly made; vilify suggests a louder, sustained campaign of abuse.

origin: From Late Latin vilificare, from vilis, 'cheap' or 'worthless', the root of vile.

definition: Extremely small, often too small to matter.
nuance: Minuscule stresses how tiny an amount, chance or object is, often to make a point: a minuscule risk, a minuscule budget. It is more emphatic than small and slightly formal. Watch the spelling: it is related to minus, so it is not 'miniscule', a very common mistake.

examples.text: The portions at that restaurant were minuscule; I was hungry again an hour later.
The chance of a large asteroid hitting Earth this century is minuscule, but scientists still track the biggest ones.
The club's budget is minuscule compared with that of the big city teams.
The changes to the contract are minuscule and do not affect your rights.
She wrote in minuscule letters so that no one could read her diary over her shoulder.
Even minuscule differences in starting conditions can lead to very different weather patterns.

cloze.text: Compared with the vast universe, our planet is not just small but ___, a mere speck of dust.
The fee is ___, less than a thousandth of a penny for every message, so most users never even notice it.
Researchers detected only a ___ trace of the chemical, thousands of times below the level that could cause harm.

misuse.text: The minuscule crowd of eighty thousand filled the stadium to the roof.
misuse.why: Minuscule means extremely small, so it cannot describe a huge crowd.

misuse.text: She was minuscule about every detail of the plan, checking each one twice.
misuse.why: Minuscule means very small; for careful attention to detail use 'meticulous'.

synonyms.vs: Tiny is everyday; minuscule is more emphatic and slightly formal.
Minute (my-NEWT) also means very small but often suggests fine detail; minuscule stresses insignificance.
Negligible means so small it can be ignored; minuscule describes size, though it often implies the same.

origin: From Latin minusculus, 'rather small', related to minus, 'less'. In English it first described small lower-case letters.

definition: A person who gives formal public speeches, especially one who is skilled and persuasive.
nuance: Orator usually praises someone's power to move or persuade an audience through speech. It is common in history and politics, where Cicero, Churchill and Martin Luther King are often called great orators. It sounds formal and slightly old-fashioned in casual talk.

examples.text: Cicero was the greatest orator of ancient Rome, famous for speeches that could sway a whole court.
Even her critics admit that she is a gifted orator who can hold a crowd for an hour.
I'm no orator, so please keep my part of the wedding speech to two minutes.
The debating society trains young orators to argue clearly under pressure.
The old orator raised one hand, and the noisy square fell silent.
Schools of rhetoric in ancient Greece taught orators to build a speech in fixed parts.

cloze.text: Not just a good speaker but a brilliant ___, he could move an audience of thousands to tears with a single speech.
Ancient Greek schools trained young men to become ___, skilled at persuading crowds and courts.
Shy in private, she became a fearless and eloquent ___ the moment she stood at the podium.

misuse.text: The orator sat silently at the back and never said a word.
misuse.why: An orator is a public speaker, so silence is the opposite of the role.

misuse.text: The orator of the novel describes his childhood in long letters.
misuse.why: The person telling a story is the narrator; an orator gives spoken public speeches.

synonyms.vs: Speaker is neutral and can mean anyone talking; an orator is a skilled, often famous public speaker.
A rhetorician studies or teaches the art of persuasion; an orator actually delivers speeches.
Speechmaker is plain and can sound dull; orator suggests eloquence and impact.

confusables.note: A narrator tells a story.
An oratorio is a large musical work for choir and orchestra.

origin: From Latin orator, 'speaker', from orare, 'to speak' or 'to pray'.

definition: Shockingly obvious and openly wrong, with no attempt to hide it.
nuance: Flagrant is used for breaches of rules, laws and rights: a flagrant violation, a flagrant abuse of power. It combines two ideas, that the act is wrong and that it is done openly. It is formal and common in law, sport and news reporting.

examples.text: The goalkeeper was sent off for a flagrant handball, grabbing the ball outside his area right in front of the referee.
The tribunal found the invasion to be a flagrant breach of international law.
Flagrant breaches of the safety rules will lead to immediate dismissal.
Parking in the ambulance bay is a flagrant breach of the rules, and you know it.
Despite the queen's ban, the duke held a feast in flagrant defiance of her orders.
The essay argues that the trials were a flagrant abuse of power, ignoring even the basic legal rules of the time.

cloze.text: Copying an entire essay from the internet is a ___ case of cheating that no teacher could miss.
The company was fined for its ___ disregard of safety laws: it ignored every warning for years.
Building a hotel on protected land, in full view of officials, was a ___ breach of the rules.

misuse.text: The garden was full of flagrant roses that smelled wonderful.
misuse.why: Flagrant means shockingly wrong; the word for a pleasant smell is 'fragrant'.

misuse.text: His flagrant mistake was so tiny that nobody noticed it.
misuse.why: Flagrant means glaringly obvious, so something nobody noticed cannot be flagrant.

synonyms.vs: Blatant stresses that something is done openly and unashamedly; flagrant adds a stronger sense of serious wrongdoing.
Glaring is used for obvious errors and omissions; flagrant for deliberate breaches of rules or rights.
Egregious means outstandingly bad, often foolish; flagrant stresses how openly the offence is committed.

confusables.note: Fragrant means sweet-smelling.

origin: From Latin flagrare, 'to blaze', as in the legal phrase in flagrante delicto, 'while the crime is blazing', meaning caught in the act.

definition: Calm and peaceful, and not easily upset or excited.
nuance: Placid describes calm people, animals and water. For people and animals it is usually approving, suggesting an even temper, though it can hint at dullness or lack of ambition. A placid lake or sea is smooth and still.

examples.text: Our new puppy is surprisingly placid; he just sleeps through thunderstorms and fireworks.
The placid surface of the lake reflected every tree on the far shore.
Farmers favoured placid breeds of cattle because they were easier and safer to handle.
Despite the chaos on the pitch, the placid manager simply folded his arms and watched.
Guide dogs are selected for a placid temperament and a willingness to work.
The novel contrasts the placid surface of village life with the secrets hidden beneath it.

cloze.text: Unlike her excitable sister, she had a naturally ___ temperament: almost nothing could upset or excite her.
After the storm passed, the sea became ___ again, as flat and still as glass.
Horses for young riders need a ___ nature: nothing should startle or excite them easily.

misuse.text: The placid crowd screamed, shoved and threw bottles at the stage.
misuse.why: Placid means calm and peaceful, the opposite of a violent, screaming crowd.

misuse.text: He tried to placid the angry customer with a free coffee.
misuse.why: Placid is an adjective; the verb for calming someone down is 'placate'.

synonyms.vs: Calm is everyday and can be temporary; placid suggests a settled, naturally even temper.
Serene suggests a peaceful, almost graceful calm; placid can hint at dullness or lack of feeling.
Tranquil is used mainly for places and scenes; placid is used for people, animals and water.

confusables.note: Placate is a verb meaning to calm someone who is angry.

origin: From Latin placidus, 'gentle' or 'calm', from placere, 'to please'.

definition: Acting on firm moral rules, or based on clear and consistent reasoning.
nuance: Principled praises people and decisions guided by moral standards even when this is costly: a principled stand, a principled refusal. In academic writing it also means based on clear rules or theory rather than convenience: a principled approach. It is approving and fairly formal.

examples.text: In a principled stand, the minister resigned rather than vote for a law she believed was wrong.
The author offers a principled way of deciding which sources to trust, instead of relying on instinct.
He's very principled; he once handed in a wallet with five hundred pounds still inside.
The board must reach a principled decision based on the evidence, not on personal loyalty.
She was too principled to lie, even to save her own brother.
Philosophers distinguish principled objections to a theory from merely practical ones.

cloze.text: She took a ___ stand, refusing a large bonus because she believed the company had treated workers unfairly.
Rather than choosing cases for convenience, the researchers used a ___ method, grounded in theory and clear, stated rules.
The judge was deeply ___, guided by firm moral rules that she refused to bend for anyone, however powerful.

misuse.text: The principled thief happily lied to everyone to get what he wanted.
misuse.why: Principled means guided by moral standards, so it does not fit someone who lies freely for gain.

misuse.text: The college's principled, Dr Jones, will give the opening speech.
misuse.why: The head of a college is the principal; principled is an adjective meaning guided by moral standards.

phrases: A more principled approach would be to...

synonyms.vs: Ethical describes behaviour that is morally right in general; principled stresses sticking to your values under pressure.
Scrupulous stresses great care to do nothing wrong; principled stresses firm, stated values.
Upright is slightly old-fashioned and describes general honesty; principled suggests standing by particular beliefs.

confusables.note: Principal means main, or the head of a school or college.

sense: impossible to defend or keep up
definition: Impossible to defend against criticism, or impossible to continue.
nuance: Untenable is common in academic writing for theories and arguments that cannot survive the evidence. In news it often describes a situation or job that cannot go on, as in 'her position became untenable', usually just before a resignation. It is formal and strongly negative.

examples.text: Once the new fossils were found, the old theory was untenable: no one could defend it any longer.
After the leaked emails, the manager's position was untenable, and he resigned the next morning.
Six people sharing one bathroom is untenable; we need a second one.
The committee considers the current arrangement untenable and recommends an urgent review.
She realised her lie had become untenable; too many people already knew the truth.
The essay argues that a strict divide between nature and nurture is untenable.

cloze.text: New evidence made his argument ___: there was no longer any way to defend it.
With half the staff refusing to work with her, the director's position became ___ and she resigned.
Surrounded and out of supplies, the soldiers found their position on the hill ___: they could no longer hold it.

misuse.text: The theory is untenable, so it has been accepted by every scientist.
misuse.why: Untenable means it cannot be defended, so scientists would reject it, not accept it.

misuse.text: The castle walls were so strong that the fortress stayed untenable for centuries.
misuse.why: Untenable means impossible to hold or defend; a fortress with strong walls is the opposite.

phrases: This view is ultimately untenable because...

synonyms.vs: Indefensible is often moral, meaning wrong and inexcusable; untenable is about logic or practicality.
Unsustainable means it cannot continue for long; untenable also means it cannot be defended in argument.
Flawed means having faults that might be fixed; untenable means it cannot be defended at all.

origin: From un- plus tenable, from French tenir, 'to hold', from Latin tenere: an untenable position cannot be held.

sense: give up power or a duty
definition: To give up a throne or position of power, or to fail to accept a duty.
nuance: Abdicate is used for monarchs who give up the throne. Figuratively, 'abdicate responsibility' is a common, critical phrase in essays and news for people or bodies that will not do their job. It is formal.

examples.text: Edward VIII abdicated in 1936, giving up the throne so that he could marry Wallis Simpson.
Residents accuse the council of abdicating its responsibility for the town's crumbling roads.
Directors must not abdicate their legal duties by leaving every decision to consultants.
Don't abdicate responsibility for the bills just because you're moving out next month.
The old king abdicates in the first chapter, and his three daughters fight over the crown.
Historians still debate why the emperor abdicated rather than fight on after the defeat.

cloze.text: Rather than rule a divided country, the king chose to ___, handing the throne to his younger brother.
Like a king giving up his crown, the school board ___ its responsibility to protect pupils, ignoring complaints for years.
The Russian emperor ___ in 1917, ending three centuries of rule by his family.

misuse.text: The prince abdicated to the throne after his father died.
misuse.why: To abdicate is to give up the throne; a new monarch accedes to it.

misuse.text: The lawyer abdicated for her client in court.
misuse.why: Speaking in support of someone is advocating; abdicate means giving up power or a duty.

synonyms.vs: Resign is used for jobs and offices; abdicate is mainly for monarchs, or figuratively for duties.
Renounce means formally giving up a claim, belief or right; abdicate is about power or responsibility.
Relinquish means letting go of something, often reluctantly; abdicate suggests giving up a role you ought to keep.

confusables.note: To advocate is to speak in favour of someone or something.

origin: From Latin abdicare, 'to renounce', from ab, 'away', and dicare, 'to proclaim'.

definition: Cool and distant towards other people, or deliberately not involved.
nuance: Aloof describes people who keep their distance, often seeming proud or unfriendly, though they may just be shy. It is usually mildly critical. In 'stay aloof from' or 'remain aloof from', it means deliberately not getting involved, for example in a dispute.

examples.text: The new boy seemed aloof at first, never joining in, but really he was just shy.
The star was criticised for being aloof with fans, refusing autographs and photos.
Britain remained aloof from the first steps towards European integration in the 1950s.
The duchess stood aloof at the edge of the ballroom, speaking to no one.
Managers who remain aloof from their teams often miss early signs of problems.
Pupils in the study rated aloof teachers as less fair, even when their grades were similar.

cloze.text: He seemed cool and ___ at the party, polite but distant, as if he thought himself above the other guests.
While her colleagues argued, she stayed coolly ___, standing apart as if the quarrel were beneath her.
Some people mistake shyness for being cold and ___, when the person is simply nervous.

misuse.text: Our aloof neighbour chats with everyone and throws a party every weekend.
misuse.why: Aloof means cool and distant, the opposite of a sociable neighbour.

misuse.text: The plane flew aloof over the mountains.
misuse.why: Aloof describes a distant manner, not height; the word for up in the air is 'aloft'.

synonyms.vs: Distant is everyday and may be temporary; aloof suggests a fixed, sometimes proud attitude.
Reserved suggests quiet and private, without unfriendliness; aloof suggests coldness or superiority.
Detached suggests emotional distance, sometimes useful and objective; aloof is more about social coldness.

confusables.note: Aloft means up in the air.

origin: Originally a sailing word, from a- plus loof, 'windward': steering into the wind kept a ship away from the shore.

sense: known or understood by very few
definition: Mysterious or obscure, and understood by only a few people with special knowledge.
nuance: Arcane is often used, sometimes critically, about rules, procedures and jargon that seem needlessly complicated to outsiders: arcane tax laws, arcane rituals. It can also suggest secret or magical knowledge. It is formal and common in journalism and essays.

examples.text: Few voters understand the arcane rules that decide how the party chooses its leader.
Medieval scribes used arcane abbreviations that modern scholars still struggle to decode.
My uncle's hobby is pretty arcane: he collects railway timetables from the 1950s.
The new handbook replaces arcane legal terms with plain English wherever possible.
The old librarian guarded a shelf of arcane books that no student was allowed to touch.
Critics argue that some literary theory is written in arcane jargon that shuts out general readers.

cloze.text: The tax rules are so ___ that only a handful of specialists in the country fully understand them.
The secret society had ___ rituals, known only to its oldest members.
Few outsiders can follow the ___ debates of medieval scholars, full of obscure terms and fine distinctions.

misuse.text: The rules are arcane, so every child can follow them easily.
misuse.why: Arcane means obscure and understood by few, the opposite of easy to follow.

misuse.text: He spent years studying the arcane of ancient magic.
misuse.why: Arcane is an adjective, not a noun; say 'arcane secrets' or 'the mysteries of'.

synonyms.vs: Obscure means little known or hard to understand; arcane adds a sense of secret or specialist knowledge.
Esoteric means meant for a small group of experts; arcane suggests mystery and often needless complexity.
Abstruse means hard to understand because it is intellectually difficult; arcane because it is secret or specialist.

origin: From Latin arcanus, 'secret' or 'hidden', from arca, 'a chest', a place where things are shut away.

sense: giving its name to a title or thing
definition: Being the person or thing that gives its name to a work, place or company.
nuance: Eponymous is used about characters, founders and artists whose names form a title: the eponymous heroine of Jane Eyre, a band's eponymous first album. It is formal and common in reviews and literary criticism. It simply points out the shared name and is neither approving nor critical.

examples.text: In Jane Eyre, the eponymous heroine tells her own story, from childhood to marriage.
The band's eponymous first album, simply called Blue Harbour, sold a million copies.
The café is called Marco's, and the eponymous Marco makes every pizza himself.
The firm's eponymous founder still chairs the board at the age of ninety.
He hated sharing a name with the eponymous villain of a children's cartoon.
Hamlet, the eponymous prince, has more lines than any other character in Shakespeare.

cloze.text: In the novel Emma, the ___ heroine shares her name with the title of the book.
Rome is said to take its name from Romulus, its ___ founder, who gave the city his own name.
Every Ford car carries the name of the company's ___ founder, Henry Ford, who gave the firm his surname.

misuse.text: The eponymous author wrote under a false name so that no one would know who she was.
misuse.why: Hiding your name makes you anonymous; eponymous means giving your name to something.

misuse.text: The film's eponymous ending surprised everyone in the cinema.
misuse.why: Eponymous refers to the person or thing a title is named after, not to a memorable part of a work.

synonyms.vs: Titular also means named in the title, but can also mean holding a title without real power.
Self-titled is used mainly for albums named after the band or artist; eponymous is broader and more formal.

confusables.note: Anonymous means with no known name.

origin: From Greek eponymos, 'given as a name', from epi, 'upon', and onyma, 'name'.

definition: Dull, uninspired and without energy, brightness or excitement.
nuance: Lacklustre is a favourite word in reviews, sports reports and business news for performances, results and campaigns that disappoint. It is critical but mild, suggesting a lack of effort or spark rather than outright failure. British English spells it lacklustre and American English lackluster.

examples.text: After a lacklustre first half with no shots on goal, the team finally came to life after the break.
The study links lacklustre economic growth in the 1970s to sharp rises in oil prices.
The film had a great cast but a lacklustre script, so I nearly fell asleep.
Sales were lacklustre in the third quarter, falling short of the forecast by 8 percent.
After weeks at sea, her hair hung lacklustre and limp around her face.
Reviewers found the sequel lacklustre, arguing that it repeated the original's ideas without any of its energy.

cloze.text: Missing the sparkle of last season, the team gave a flat, ___ performance, with tired players and not a single good chance.
Despite heavy advertising, sales of the new phone were ___: not a disaster, but flat and without any spark of excitement.
His ___ speech, read flatly from notes, failed to inspire anyone in the hall.

misuse.text: The lacklustre fireworks lit up the sky in a thrilling, dazzling display.
misuse.why: Lacklustre means dull and uninspiring, so it contradicts a thrilling, dazzling display.

misuse.text: The new striker lacklustre in his first match and was dropped.
misuse.why: Lacklustre is an adjective, not a verb; say he played poorly or gave a lacklustre performance.

synonyms.vs: Dull is everyday and broad; lacklustre suggests something that should have been lively but disappointed.
Uninspired stresses a lack of new ideas; lacklustre stresses a lack of energy or spark.
Mediocre means only average in quality; lacklustre focuses on flatness and lack of energy.

origin: Made from lack and lustre, 'shine'. Shakespeare wrote of a 'lack-lustre eye' in As You Like It.

definition: According to what is claimed or reported, though it has not been proved.
nuance: Purportedly signals that a claim comes from someone else and has not been checked, so the writer keeps a careful distance. It is formal and common in news and academic writing about documents, origins and effects. It is close to 'supposedly' but sounds more neutral and less mocking.

examples.text: The painting, purportedly by Rembrandt, turned out to be a skilled copy made a century later.
The letter, purportedly written by the queen herself, may in fact be a later forgery.
This café purportedly does the best brownies in town, so let's test that claim.
The email, purportedly from the bank, asked customers to confirm their passwords.
He carried a faded map that purportedly showed the way to a buried fortune.
The diet purportedly reduces stress, but the trials supporting it were very small.

cloze.text: The diary claims to be a soldier's account of 1916: it was ___ written in the trenches, but experts suspect a modern forgery.
The text message ___ came from the delivery company, but it was really a scam.
The new supplement ___ boosts memory, though no proper trial has ever tested the claim.

misuse.text: The results were purportedly confirmed by three independent laboratories, so we know for certain they are true.
misuse.why: Purportedly signals an unproven claim, so it clashes with saying the facts are certain.

misuse.text: He broke the vase purportedly, just to annoy his sister.
misuse.why: Purportedly means 'reportedly', not 'on purpose'; for a deliberate act use 'purposely' or 'deliberately'.

synonyms.vs: Allegedly is used especially for accusations of wrongdoing; purportedly for claims about origins, authorship or effects.
Supposedly is more informal and often openly doubtful; purportedly sounds neutral.
Reportedly means according to reports, often in the media; purportedly stresses what a thing or person claims to be.

confusables.note: Purposely means deliberately, on purpose.

definition: Not hurt, harmed or damaged, especially after a dangerous or difficult event.
nuance: Unscathed is common in news and sport after crashes, storms, crises and scandals: someone walked away or emerged unscathed. It usually follows verbs like 'escape', 'emerge' and 'survive'. It can describe reputations and finances as well as bodies.

examples.text: Both drivers walked away from the crash unscathed, though their cars were badly damaged.
Few industries emerged from the 2008 financial crisis unscathed.
I fell off my bike in the rain but somehow got home unscathed.
The university's research funding has so far survived the budget cuts unscathed.
The old oak stood unscathed after the storm, while every fence around it lay flat.
Historians note that the cathedral survived the bombing almost unscathed, while the streets around it were destroyed.

cloze.text: Amazingly, the cat survived a fall from the third floor completely ___, without a single scratch.
Her career emerged ___ from the scandal: within a year she had been promoted.
Few towns on the coast escaped the hurricane ___; most lost roofs, roads or power.

misuse.text: The unscathed driver was taken to hospital with serious injuries.
misuse.why: Unscathed means not harmed at all, so it contradicts serious injuries.

misuse.text: The critic wrote an unscathed review, attacking every scene of the film.
misuse.why: A harsh, attacking review is 'scathing'; unscathed means unharmed.

synonyms.vs: Unharmed is plain and literal; unscathed is livelier and often used after a dramatic escape.
Unhurt is everyday and used for people's bodies; unscathed also covers reputations, careers and finances.
Intact describes things that remain whole and complete; unscathed is used more for people and what happens to them.

confusables.note: Scathing means harshly critical.

origin: From un- plus scathe, an old word for harm or injury, which also gives us scathing.

definition: Very eager and committed to a cause or task, sometimes too much.
nuance: Zealous describes strong, energetic devotion to a cause, job or belief. It can be approving (a zealous campaigner) but often hints at going too far, as in 'over-zealous' officials. It is formal and common in history and news.

examples.text: A zealous traffic warden gave out forty parking tickets in a single morning.
Zealous reformers in the sixteenth century destroyed many church paintings and statues.
My brother is a zealous recycler; he even washes out yoghurt pots.
The firm has been zealous in protecting its customers' personal data.
The young doctor was zealous in her work, visiting every patient on the ward before breakfast.
Some historians argue that zealous enforcement of the ban turned public opinion against it.

cloze.text: Full of fiery enthusiasm for the cause, the ___ campaigners knocked on every door in town.
The new inspector is almost too ___ about the rules, eagerly checking every receipt himself.
Their ___ efforts to convert everyone they met, however passionate, made some neighbours uncomfortable.

misuse.text: He was so zealous about the project that he skipped most of the meetings.
misuse.why: Zealous means very eager and committed, which does not fit someone who skips meetings.

misuse.text: She felt zealous when her best friend won the prize she wanted.
misuse.why: Resenting what someone else has is being 'jealous'; zealous means eagerly committed.

synonyms.vs: Enthusiastic is everyday and positive; zealous is stronger and can suggest excessive commitment.
Fervent stresses intense feeling or belief; zealous stresses energetic action for a cause.
Ardent suggests warm, passionate support; zealous suggests determined, sometimes overbearing activity.
Fanatical is clearly negative and extreme; zealous can still be approving.

confusables.note: Jealous means resentful of what others have; the two words share a Greek root.

origin: From Greek zelos, 'zeal' or 'eager rivalry', through Latin; jealous comes from the same root.

sense: the origin and history of a word
definition: The origin and history of a word, or the study of where words come from.
nuance: Etymology is used in linguistics, literature and everyday curiosity about language. 'The etymology of X' means where that word comes from, while 'etymology' alone can mean the field of study. Do not confuse it with entomology, the study of insects.

examples.text: I love the etymology of 'salary': it's linked to the Latin word for salt.
Tracing the etymology of 'nice' shows how its meaning shifted from 'foolish' to 'pleasant' over the centuries.
Etymologies can mislead, since a word's origin rarely tells us how it is used today.
A new online dictionary lets readers explore the etymology of every entry with a single click.
Each entry in the glossary gives a definition, a pronunciation and a brief etymology.
The professor opened every lecture with an etymology, as if each word were a small mystery to solve.

cloze.text: According to its ___, the word 'disaster' comes from old words meaning 'bad star'.
A folk ___ is a false story about where a word comes from, such as the myth that 'posh' stands for 'port out, starboard home'.
Her new book is not about entomology, the study of insects, but about ___, the study of where words come from.

misuse.text: She studied etymology because she wanted to learn about beetles and butterflies.
misuse.why: The study of insects is entomology; etymology is about the origins of words.

misuse.text: The etymology of the river is a small spring high in the mountains.
misuse.why: Etymology is the origin of words, not of rivers or other things; use 'source'.

synonyms.vs: Derivation is how a word is formed from another, often within one language; etymology is a word's full history.
Origin is general and works for anything; etymology is only for words.
Philology is the broader study of languages and texts over time; etymology focuses on individual words.

confusables.note: Entomology is the study of insects.

origin: From Greek etymologia, from etymon, 'true sense', and -logia, 'study': the study of a word's true meaning.

sense: a servile follower of someone powerful
definition: A person who obeys a powerful person too eagerly, doing whatever they are told.
nuance: Lackey is an insult: calling someone a lackey says they have no independence and simply serve someone more powerful. It is common in commentary, history and fiction. Its older meaning was a uniformed male servant or footman.

examples.text: The tyrant surrounded himself with lackeys who praised every decision and never dared to disagree.
In the novel, the governor's lackeys carry out his cruelties so that he can keep his own hands clean.
I'm not your lackey; fetch your own coffee for once.
Critics dismissed the new board as a group of lackeys hand-picked by the owner.
Historians once saw the duke as a mere lackey of the crown, but his letters show he often defied it.
The report concludes that the inspector acted independently and was no lackey of the company.

cloze.text: Fearing independent thought, the dictator kept only obedient ___ around him, people who would do anything to please him.
He refused to be anyone's ___, fetching coffee and laughing at bad jokes just to keep his job.
Critics called the spokesman a mere ___ of the company, eager to run any errand and obey any order his bosses gave.

misuse.text: As the most powerful person in the company, the chairman was everyone's lackey.
misuse.why: A lackey serves someone more powerful, so the most powerful person cannot be one.

misuse.text: Thank you for being such a wonderful lackey; the whole team admires you.
misuse.why: Lackey is an insult suggesting servility, so it does not work as praise; say 'assistant' or 'helper'.

synonyms.vs: A sycophant flatters to win favour; a lackey mainly obeys and does the dirty work.
Underling means someone of lower rank, mildly contemptuous; lackey stresses slavish obedience.
Stooge suggests someone used or manipulated by others, often foolishly; lackey suggests willing servility.
Minion is often humorous for a follower or helper; lackey is a sharper insult.

origin: Originally a footman or uniformed servant, from French laquais.

sense: make weaker or smaller in effect
definition: To make something weaker, thinner or smaller in force, effect or amount.
nuance: Attenuate is formal and common in science, medicine and engineering, where signals, sounds and effects are attenuated. Attenuated vaccines contain a weakened form of a virus. In general academic writing it means reducing the strength of an effect or link.

examples.text: Thick stone attenuates the noise from the street, so the library stays quiet even at rush hour.
Many vaccines use an attenuated virus, weakened so that it cannot cause serious illness.
The new flood barriers attenuated the force of the waves, protecting homes along the coast.
Regular exercise appears to have an attenuating effect on stress, reducing its impact on the heart.
My new headphones attenuate the engine hum, so I can actually sleep on flights.
As the ship sailed further out, the radio signal attenuated to a faint crackle.

cloze.text: Thick curtains ___ the sound of traffic, reducing it to a faint hum.
The vaccine contains an ___ virus, one weakened in the lab so that it cannot cause disease.
Engineers measure in decibels how much each kilometre of cable ___ the signal, so they know where to place boosters.

misuse.text: The fresh evidence attenuated her argument, making it much stronger than before.
misuse.why: Attenuate means weaken, so it contradicts making an argument stronger.

misuse.text: Please attenuate the meeting at nine tomorrow morning.
misuse.why: Being present is 'attend'; attenuate means to weaken or reduce something.

synonyms.vs: Weaken is everyday and general; attenuate is technical and often used for signals, effects and forces.
Diminish means to become or make smaller; attenuate stresses thinning or weakening of strength.
Dampen is used for enthusiasm, sounds or vibrations; attenuate is more formal and scientific.

confusables.note: Extenuating circumstances make a wrong seem less serious.

origin: From Latin attenuare, 'to make thin', from tenuis, 'thin', the root of tenuous.

sense: a sign that something is coming
definition: A person or thing that signals that something, often important, is about to happen.
nuance: Harbinger is usually followed by 'of': a harbinger of spring, change or doom. It is formal and slightly literary, common in news analysis and history. It can announce good or bad things, though 'harbinger of doom' is a well-worn phrase.

examples.text: The dark clouds piling up over the hills were a harbinger of the storm that hit the village that night.
Economists see the fall in house sales as a harbinger of a wider slowdown.
Some historians treat the revolt of 1381 as a harbinger of the end of serfdom in England.
That grey sky is a harbinger of doom for our picnic, I reckon.
Rising absence rates may be early harbingers of deeper problems in a team.
Small changes in soil chemistry can act as harbingers of much larger environmental damage.

cloze.text: The first snowdrops are a ___ of spring, appearing just before the weather turns warm.
The sudden cash shortage proved a ___ of the bank's collapse, which came two months later.
Ravens were once seen as ___ of death, birds that announced disaster before it struck.

misuse.text: The flood was a harbinger of the heavy rain that caused it.
misuse.why: A harbinger comes before what it announces; heavy rain can be a harbinger of a flood, not the other way round.

misuse.text: The muddy footprints were a harbinger that the burglar had already been and gone.
misuse.why: A harbinger signals something still to come; evidence of something that has already happened is a sign or a clue.

synonyms.vs: Sign is everyday and general; harbinger specifically signals something still to come.
A precursor comes before and leads to something; a harbinger mainly announces or warns of it.
An omen is a mystical sign of future good or evil; harbinger is broader and more factual.
Herald is close but more often used for good news or something new arriving.

origin: First a person sent ahead of an army or royal party to find lodgings; from Old French herberge, 'lodging'.

sense: say unfair, harmful things about someone
definition: To say unpleasant things about someone or something that are untrue or unfair.
nuance: Malign is formal and suggests that the criticism is unfair, often false. It is most common in the passive: something or someone is 'unfairly maligned' or 'much maligned'. As an adjective, malign also means harmful, as in 'a malign influence'.

examples.text: The new stadium, maligned by locals for years, has in fact brought thousands of visitors to the town.
Many historians argue that Richard III has been unfairly maligned, largely by writers working under the Tudors.
Stop maligning my cooking; you had two helpings!
Employees should not malign competitors in conversations with clients.
He maligns everyone who leaves the village, as if leaving were a crime.
Once maligned as a waste of time, video games are now studied for their effects on problem-solving.

cloze.text: The much-___ school dinner, long mocked as grey and tasteless, has in fact improved enormously in recent years.
Pigeons are often unfairly ___ as dirty pests, though they are clean and remarkably clever birds.
It is wrong to ___ a whole profession with false and unfair claims because of the mistakes of a few.

misuse.text: The coach maligned his star player, praising her skill and dedication in every interview.
misuse.why: To malign is to speak badly and unfairly of someone, not to praise them.

misuse.text: The vet said the lump on the dog's leg was maligned and must be removed.
misuse.why: A harmful tumour is 'malignant'; maligned means unfairly criticised.

synonyms.vs: Criticise can be fair; malign implies the criticism is unjust or untrue.
Slander is a legal term for false spoken statements; malign is broader and less technical.
Disparage means to belittle or play down; malign suggests harmful, often false claims.
Vilify suggests loud, abusive attacks; malign is quieter and stresses unfairness.

confusables.note: Malignant describes a harmful tumour or an evil influence.

origin: From Latin malignus, 'wicked' or 'spiteful', from malus, 'bad'.

definition: Bitterly harsh and mocking, in a way meant to sting or hurt.
nuance: Caustic describes remarks, wit, humour and reviews that sting. It can be admired as clever as well as criticised as cruel. Its literal meaning, in chemistry, is able to burn or eat away, as in caustic soda.

examples.text: Her caustic comments about my haircut made me want to hide under a hat for a week.
The critic's caustic review called the musical 'three hours of noise in search of a tune'.
Swift's caustic satire attacked the cruelty of English policy towards Ireland.
The judge made caustic remarks about the poor quality of the evidence.
'How generous of you,' she said, in a caustic tone that froze the whole table.
Wilde's caustic wit exposed the hypocrisy of polite Victorian society.

cloze.text: His ___ wit made audiences laugh, but it left many of his targets deeply hurt.
The review was ___, mocking every line of dialogue with bitter sarcasm.
Like a chemical that burns the skin, her ___ remarks left a lasting sting.

misuse.text: His caustic praise warmed everyone's heart.
misuse.why: Caustic means bitterly harsh and mocking, so it cannot describe heartwarming praise.

misuse.text: She was caustic about crossing the busy road, checking both ways three times.
misuse.why: Being careful is being 'cautious'; caustic means harsh and biting.

synonyms.vs: Sarcastic means saying the opposite of what you mean to mock; caustic is broader and suggests burning harshness.
Acerbic is close but suggests sharp, sour wit; caustic sounds more corrosive and hurtful.
Scathing is used for strongly critical judgements; caustic for a habitually biting tone or wit.

confusables.note: Cautious means careful to avoid danger.

origin: From Greek kaustikos, 'burning', from kaiein, 'to burn'.

sense: looking at your own thoughts and feelings
definition: The careful examination of your own thoughts, feelings and reasons for acting.
nuance: Introspection is often seen as healthy self-reflection and a route to self-knowledge, but too much can suggest brooding or self-absorption. In psychology it is also a research method in which people report their own mental processes. It often follows a failure or crisis: 'a period of introspection'.

examples.text: After the breakup, I spent weeks in introspection, asking myself what I could have done differently.
Early psychologists relied on introspection, asking trained observers to describe their own sensations.
The heavy defeat led to a period of introspection at the club about its future.
The course encourages introspection, asking students to consider how their values shape their decisions.
The long train journey was a time for introspection, and she watched the fields pass in silence.
Critics question whether introspection gives reliable access to the real causes of our behaviour.

cloze.text: Keeping a journal encourages ___, the habit of looking inward at your own thoughts and motives.
After losing the election, the party went through a long period of ___, asking itself what had gone wrong.
Philosophers have long debated how far ___, examining one's own mind from the inside, can be trusted.

misuse.text: The doctor's introspection of the patient's throat revealed an infection.
misuse.why: Introspection is examining your own mind; a doctor examining a patient carries out an inspection or examination.

misuse.text: He was full of introspection about other people's problems.
misuse.why: Introspection looks inward at your own thoughts, not at other people's problems.

synonyms.vs: Self-reflection is broad and positive; introspection is more formal and can hint at brooding.
Self-examination often has a moral angle, judging your own conduct; introspection observes thoughts and feelings.
Contemplation is thoughtful attention to anything; introspection is directed at your own mind.

confusables.note: An inspection is a careful look at something or someone else.

origin: From Latin introspicere, 'to look inside', from intro, 'within', and specere, 'to look'.

definition: To admire or love someone so much that you cannot see any faults in them.
nuance: Idolise is used for fans, children and followers who admire someone without question: a pop star, a footballer, an older sister. It often hints that the admiration is excessive or naive. British English usually spells it idolise and American English idolize.

examples.text: My little brother idolises his football coach and copies everything he does, even the way he walks.
The singer, idolised by millions of teenagers, announced her retirement at just twenty-six.
The study explores why adolescents idolise celebrities more intensely than adults do.
She had idolised her father as a child, so his betrayal hit her twice as hard.
Idolising a leader can make followers blind to obvious mistakes.
Romantic poets were idolised by their readers, who copied their clothes and even their moods.

cloze.text: As a boy he used to ___ the astronaut, covering his walls with her posters and believing she could do no wrong.
Fans who blindly ___ a celebrity often refuse to believe any criticism of them.
The young players ___ their captain, treating his every word as if it were perfect.

misuse.text: He idolised his rival so much that he never missed a chance to insult him.
misuse.why: To idolise is to admire someone hugely, not to dislike or insult them.

misuse.text: She spent the whole of Sunday idolising on the sofa.
misuse.why: Idolise means admiring someone too much; lazing about doing nothing is 'idling'.

synonyms.vs: Admire is moderate and often reasoned; idolise means admiring without question, seeing no faults.
Worship is used for gods and, informally, heroes; idolise is the usual word for celebrities and role models.
Revere suggests deep, solemn respect, often for the wise or holy; idolise suggests excited, uncritical devotion.

confusables.note: Idle (it sounds like idol) means lazy or not in use.

origin: From idol, through Latin idolum, from Greek eidolon, 'image', first meaning an image worshipped as a god.

sense: the whole body of work of an artist or writer
definition: The complete body of work produced by a writer, artist or composer, seen as a whole.
nuance: Oeuvre is a French loan used in criticism, art history and reviews to talk about everything a creator has made. It lets you discuss patterns across a whole career rather than a single book or painting. It is usually singular, as in 'her oeuvre', and sounds odd for everyday output such as emails.

examples.text: Across her whole oeuvre, from early short stories to her final novels, Toni Morrison keeps returning to memory and loss.
The festival celebrates two directors whose oeuvres could hardly be more different.
Of all the films in his oeuvre, I still think the first one is the funniest.
Scholars have long debated whether the late romances fit with the rest of Shakespeare's oeuvre or stand apart.
The trust was established to catalogue and preserve the artist's oeuvre after her death.
Sitting in his studio, the old sculptor realised with a smile that his entire oeuvre fitted on one shelf.

cloze.text: The critic's book surveys the director's entire ___, his whole body of work from his first short film to his last feature.
Admirers of the poet's wider ___, her complete body of work, will find its themes of exile already present in these early letters.
This bright, crowded painting is unusual within his ___, which is otherwise made up of quiet landscapes.

misuse.text: I have a huge oeuvre of homework to finish before Monday.
misuse.why: Oeuvre means the whole body of an artist's or writer's work, not a large amount of tasks.

misuse.text: The chef's oeuvre tonight is a lemon tart with fresh cream.
misuse.why: An oeuvre is a creator's whole output over time, not one dish; 'chef-d'oeuvre' is a different word meaning masterpiece.

phrases: Within the author's wider oeuvre, this novel...
Across his oeuvre, a recurring theme is...

synonyms.vs: Body of work is the plain English equivalent; oeuvre sounds more literary and is common in criticism.
Output stresses quantity and is used for factories as well as artists; oeuvre suggests artistic achievement taken as a whole.
A canon is a set of works accepted as important, often by many authors; an oeuvre is one creator's work.

confusables.note: A small savoury dish served before a meal; it contains the same French word but means nothing similar.

origin: From French oeuvre, 'work', which comes from Latin opera, 'works'.

definition: To tell someone firmly that they have done wrong or should behave differently.
nuance: Admonish is a formal word for a firm but controlled telling-off, often from someone in authority such as a judge, teacher or referee. It is milder than 'condemn' and calmer than 'berate', and can also mean urging someone to do something. It is often passive: 'he was admonished for...'.

examples.text: The teacher admonished the boys for talking during the exam and moved them to separate desks.
The judge admonishes the jury each evening not to read news reports about the trial.
Please don't admonish me in front of everyone; just tell me quietly later.
Medieval sermons frequently admonished listeners to give up gambling and heavy drinking.
Staff who repeatedly ignore safety rules may be formally admonished before any further action is taken.
Rather than admonishing pupils in public, the school now encourages private conversations about behaviour.

cloze.text: The headteacher ___ the pupils for their rudeness, firmly but calmly, and then let them return to class.
Her supervisor ___ her for missing the deadline: a firm, formal telling-off, but no official warning.
The chair had to ___ several members for talking over each other, reminding them sternly of the rules.

misuse.text: The coach admonished the team for their brilliant win and bought everyone dinner.
misuse.why: Admonish means to scold or warn about wrongdoing; for praise use 'commended' or 'congratulated'.

misuse.text: She admonished at him for being late again.
misuse.why: Admonish takes a direct object: 'admonished him', not 'admonished at him'.

phrases: The author admonishes readers not to...

synonyms.vs: Reprimand is more official, often a formal punishment at work; admonish can be a simple firm warning.
Rebuke is sharper and more severe; admonish is calmer and meant to correct.
Scold is everyday and often used about children; admonish sounds formal and measured.
Caution means warning about a danger or risk; admonish suggests disapproval of behaviour.

origin: From Latin admonere, 'to remind' or 'to warn', through Old French.

sense: calm someone who is angry or upset
definition: To calm someone who is angry or upset, often by giving them something they want.
nuance: Pacify is used about angry people, crying babies, restless crowds and unhappy voters, often with a hint that the calm is only temporary and the problem is soothed rather than solved. In older history writing, 'pacifying' a region meant bringing it under control by force, so read that use critically.

examples.text: The baby screamed until her dad pacified her with a bottle of warm milk.
The government hopes the extra funding will pacify angry farmers before the election.
The study found that parents spend less time pacifying a crying baby once they learn to read its signals.
He's not really sorry; he only said it to pacify you.
The company pacifies unhappy customers with vouchers instead of fixing the faulty product.
Some historians argue that the reforms pacified the workers without changing who held power.

cloze.text: The furious customer refused to be ___, even when the manager offered a full refund and a free meal.
The council's review was a gesture to ___ angry residents and keep them calm, though nothing actually changed.
The club tried to ___ its furious fans with cheaper season tickets, but the protests went on.

misuse.text: The loud music pacified the crowd until they were all shouting and pushing.
misuse.why: Pacify means to make calm; shouting and pushing is the opposite.

misuse.text: The medicine pacified his broken leg so that it could heal properly.
misuse.why: Pacify is used about calming upset people, not injuries healing; say the medicine 'eased the pain'.

phrases: The concession was designed to pacify...
...a gesture intended to pacify critics rather than...

synonyms.vs: Appease means giving in to demands to keep someone quiet, often said critically; pacify focuses on the calming result.
Placate is very close but is about adults' anger and demands; pacify also suits crying babies and restless crowds.
Soothe is gentle and kind, about pain or feelings; pacify suggests settling anger or unrest.

origin: From Latin pacificare, 'to make peace', from pax, 'peace'.

definition: Cheerful and optimistic, with spirits that stay high even when things go wrong.
nuance: Buoyant first meant able to float, and this sense keeps that feeling of lightness: spirits that bob back up after a setback. It describes people, moods, spirits and voices, and is approving. Business news also calls strong, rising markets or sales 'buoyant', the same idea applied to confidence and prices.

examples.text: Despite losing his job, Tom stayed buoyant, sure that something better would come along soon.
The manager sounded buoyant after the defeat, insisting that his young team would learn from it.
Soldiers' letters home were often buoyant in tone, hiding their real fears from anxious families.
You seem very buoyant today; did you get your results back?
The annual survey found that staff morale remained buoyant despite the recent changes.
She left the interview in a buoyant mood, humming all the way to the station.

cloze.text: Like a cork that always bobs back to the surface, his spirits stayed ___ through every setback.
Her ___ mood lifted the whole office: she seemed to float through the day, humming and joking.
Not even a week of rain could sink her ___ spirits, and she stayed cheerful all holiday.

misuse.text: The mourners were buoyant as they followed the coffin in silence.
misuse.why: Buoyant means cheerful and optimistic, which does not suit a sad, silent funeral; 'sombre' fits.

misuse.text: She was buoyant all week, bursting into tears at every small disappointment.
misuse.why: Buoyant means cheerful and quick to recover, so crying at every disappointment is the opposite.

synonyms.vs: Optimistic is about expecting good things; buoyant also suggests energy and a light, lifted mood.
Cheerful is everyday and about visible good humour; buoyant suggests spirits that stay up despite setbacks.
Upbeat is informal and everyday; buoyant is a little more formal and suggests spirits that bounce back.

definition: Relating to the words of a language, rather than its grammar or sounds.
nuance: Lexical is a technical but widely used term in linguistics, language teaching and psychology. It contrasts with 'grammatical' and 'phonological', so it narrows a discussion to vocabulary itself. In everyday writing 'vocabulary' or 'word' usually sounds more natural.

examples.text: Lexical skills, such as knowing many words and their exact meanings, strongly predict reading success.
The study measured lexical development by counting how many new words toddlers used each month.
The new dictionary edition reflects lexical changes driven by social media, from 'selfie' to 'doomscrolling'.
I lost marks for lexical errors, basically using posh words in the wrong way.
Candidates are assessed on grammatical accuracy and lexical range in both the written and spoken papers.
She loved crosswords for their lexical tricks, the way one word could hide inside another.

cloze.text: The exam marks ___ range, meaning how varied and precise your choice of words is.
Unlike grammatical mistakes, ___ errors involve choosing the wrong word altogether.
Linguists compared the ___ content of the two languages by listing shared words for numbers and body parts.

misuse.text: Her handwriting is beautifully lexical and very easy to read.
misuse.why: Lexical means relating to words and vocabulary, not to how neatly something is written.

misuse.text: The speech was very lexical, full of clear arguments and sound reasoning.
misuse.why: Lexical does not mean well argued; the writer probably meant 'logical'.

phrases: At the lexical level, the text...

synonyms.vs: Verbal can mean spoken or relating to words in general; lexical is technical and refers specifically to vocabulary.
Semantic is about meaning; lexical is about the words themselves, their forms as well as meanings.

origin: From Greek lexis, 'word' or 'speech', through lexikon, 'a book of words'.

definition: Deserving praise, reward or respect because of good qualities or actions.
nuance: Meritorious is formal and mostly found in official contexts: awards, citations, legal judgements and assessments. It sounds stiff in conversation, where 'impressive' or 'admirable' is more natural. In law, a 'meritorious claim' is one with real substance behind it.

examples.text: The firefighter received a medal for meritorious conduct after rescuing three children from the blaze.
Students whose first-year work is judged meritorious may apply for an additional scholarship.
Imperial China's exams were meant to promote meritorious candidates, not just those from powerful families.
Washing up after everyone else? How very meritorious of you!
The old soldier kept his certificate for meritorious service in a frame above the fireplace.
The essay argues that the award system rewarded loyalty more often than genuinely meritorious research.

cloze.text: The police officer received an official award for ___ conduct: actions judged to deserve formal praise.
Only claims judged ___, with real evidence behind them, will go forward to a full hearing.
The prize goes to the most ___ project, the one whose quality most deserves reward, whatever the fame of its authors.

misuse.text: The meritorious crime shocked the whole town.
misuse.why: Meritorious means deserving praise, so it cannot describe a crime.

misuse.text: Her meritorious was finally recognised at the ceremony.
misuse.why: Meritorious is an adjective; the noun is 'merit', as in 'her merit was recognised'.

phrases: The proposal is meritorious in that...

synonyms.vs: Praiseworthy is plainer and more everyday; meritorious sounds official, as on medals and citations.
Commendable often praises effort or intention; meritorious suggests the result itself deserves reward.
Worthy is broader and can sound dull or earnest; meritorious specifically means deserving praise.

confusables.note: Meretricious means attractive on the surface but of no real value, almost the opposite.

definition: Coming or happening later than it should have.
nuance: Belated is often used about thanks, apologies, greetings and recognition that arrive after the right moment. It can be gentle ('belated birthday wishes') or critical ('a belated response to the crisis'). It describes the thing that is late, not a person: 'a belated apology' is natural, but 'he was belated' is not.

examples.text: I forgot her birthday last week, so I sent a belated card with an apology inside.
The government's belated response to the floods drew criticism from local councils.
Rosalind Franklin's contribution to discovering the structure of DNA has received belated recognition.
Please accept my belated thanks for your help with last month's conference.
The letter arrived three years late, a belated reply from a man she had long given up on.
Historians describe the reform as a belated attempt to modernise an army that had already been defeated.

cloze.text: Happy ___ birthday! Sorry this message is three days late.
Months after it should have said sorry, the council finally issued a ___ apology to residents.
The award was a ___ honour for a scientist whose work was ignored for decades.

misuse.text: The train was belated by twenty minutes because of signal problems.
misuse.why: Belated describes things like thanks or replies that come too late; for transport running behind time, say 'delayed'.

misuse.text: She is always belated for her morning classes.
misuse.why: Belated describes things such as apologies or wishes, not people; say she is always late.

phrases: The reform was a belated response to...

synonyms.vs: Late is the everyday word for anything after time; belated suggests something owed, like thanks, that came too late.
Overdue stresses that something should already have happened; belated describes it once it finally comes.
Tardy is formal or old-fashioned and often blames a person for being slow.

confusables.note: Berated means scolded angrily; it looks similar but has nothing to do with time.

definition: Able to judge well, especially about quality, and to notice fine differences that others miss.
nuance: Discerning is approving and describes people, tastes, readers, buyers and eyes. Advertisers love it ('for the discerning traveller'), so it can sound a little like a sales pitch. In essays it praises careful judgement, as in 'a discerning critic'.

examples.text: A discerning reader will notice that the narrator's story keeps changing in small but telling ways.
The boutique hotel caters for discerning guests who want quiet luxury rather than nightlife.
My nan is a very discerning tea drinker; she can spot a cheap brand at the first sip.
Discerning historians treat such diaries with care, since their writers often had reasons to exaggerate.
The panel will be looking for discerning judgement as well as technical skill.
With a discerning eye, the old dealer spotted the one genuine painting among a dozen fakes.

cloze.text: The shop stocks rare teas for ___ customers who can taste the subtle difference.
It takes a ___ eye, with real taste and judgement, to tell the original painting from the expert copy.
Older viewers are more ___ than advertisers think: they judge quality carefully and spot cheap tricks at once.

misuse.text: It was very discerning to see the bridge shaking in the strong wind.
misuse.why: Discerning means showing good judgement; something unsettling is 'disconcerting'.

misuse.text: He is a discerning eater who will happily eat anything put in front of him.
misuse.why: Discerning means choosy with good judgement, so eating anything at all is the opposite.

synonyms.vs: Perceptive is about noticing and understanding quickly; discerning stresses good judgement and taste.
Astute suggests shrewdness, often to gain an advantage; discerning is about fine judgement of quality.
Selective just means choosy; discerning implies that the choices are wise.

confusables.note: Disconcerting means unsettling or worrying.

origin: From Latin discernere, 'to separate' or 'to tell apart'.

definition: Filled with extreme, often unreasonable enthusiasm for a belief, cause or activity.
nuance: Fanatical is usually critical when used about politics or religion, suggesting zeal that ignores reason or tolerance. Used about hobbies and sport it can be light and even affectionate ('a fanatical gardener'). The context decides whether it is a warning or a joke.

examples.text: He is fanatical about his bike: he cleans it every day and nobody else may touch it.
The historian traces how a small but fanatical movement gained influence during the economic crisis.
Fanatical supporters queued outside the stadium overnight to buy tickets for the final.
Her fanatical attention to detail made her a brilliant but exhausting editor.
The report warns that online forums can push isolated young people towards fanatical views.
My uncle is a fanatical birdwatcher who once drove six hours to see a single owl.

cloze.text: He is ___ about fitness, with the zeal of a true believer: he trains even on Christmas Day.
The cult demanded ___ devotion, a wild zeal that left no room for doubt, and members who asked questions were thrown out.
Ordinary voters grew wary of the party's most ___ members, whose extreme, unreasoning devotion to the cause ruled out any compromise.

misuse.text: She was fanatical about the film and found it rather boring.
misuse.why: Fanatical means wildly enthusiastic, so it clashes with finding something boring.

misuse.text: The weather was fanatical, with sunshine one minute and hail the next.
misuse.why: Fanatical describes extreme devotion; changeable weather is 'erratic', and strange, dreamlike things are 'fantastical'.

synonyms.vs: Zealous is energetic devotion that can be positive; fanatical suggests it has gone too far.
