Obsessive stresses an unhealthy focus on one thing; fanatical stresses passionate devotion, especially to a cause.
Extremist is about political or religious views far from the mainstream; fanatical is about the intensity of feeling.

confusables.note: Fantastical means strange, imaginary or like a fantasy.

origin: From Latin fanaticus, 'of a temple', used of people thought to be driven wild by a god.

definition: A supply of something that is much bigger than needed, often causing prices to fall.
nuance: Glut is common in economics and business news about oil, housing, graduates or crops. It is critical or concerned in tone, suggesting waste or falling prices. It is usually followed by 'of': 'a glut of cheap phones'.

examples.text: After a perfect summer, farmers faced a glut of strawberries and had to sell them at half price.
The paper argues that a global glut of savings helped keep interest rates low in the early 2000s.
We've got a glut of courgettes again this year, so please take some home with you!
Recurring gluts and shortages made farming incomes deeply unpredictable in the 1930s.
The report warns of a glut of office space now that many staff work from home.
There was such a glut of volunteers that year that half of them were sent home with nothing to do.

cloze.text: Prices collapsed because of a ___ of grain: farmers simply grew far more than anyone could buy.
When producers pumped far more oil than the world needed, the resulting ___ sent prices crashing.
Too many students trained as lawyers, creating a ___ of graduates and too few jobs.

misuse.text: There was a glut of food in the region, so thousands of people went hungry.
misuse.why: A glut is too much of something, so it would not cause hunger; 'shortage' was meant.

misuse.text: She felt a sudden glut of sadness when her best friend moved away.
misuse.why: Glut is used about supplies of goods, money or things on offer, not feelings; use 'wave' or 'rush'.

phrases: A glut of... led to falling prices.

synonyms.vs: Surplus is neutral or even positive; glut suggests an unwanted excess that causes problems.
Oversupply is a technical term; glut is more vivid and common in journalism.
Surfeit is literary and often about too much food or pleasure.

sense: a small remaining trace of something
definition: A small part or trace of something that remains after the rest has gone.
nuance: Vestige is formal and common in history, politics and science writing about what is left of old systems, customs or feelings. It is often used with a negative, as in 'without a vestige of doubt', or in 'the last vestiges of empire'. It is usually followed by 'of'.

examples.text: A few crumbling walls are the only vestige of the castle that once stood on this hill.
Linguists regard the silent 'k' in 'knight' as a vestige of an older pronunciation.
The last vestiges of the old regime disappeared when the new constitution came into force.
He spoke without a vestige of regret, as if the betrayal had never happened.
He's lost every vestige of his Scottish accent since moving to London.
The human tailbone is often described as one of the vestiges of the tails our distant ancestors had.

cloze.text: The monarch's ceremonial role is a ___ of the age when kings held real power: the form survives, but the power has gone.
Over the next century, reforms swept away the last ___ of feudalism: small leftover customs from a system that had once ruled the whole country.
The appendix was long thought to be a useless ___ of our evolutionary past, a leftover organ with no job.

misuse.text: The new skyscraper is a proud vestige of the city's future.
misuse.why: A vestige is a remaining trace of the past, not a sign of the future.

misuse.text: The museum vestiges ancient pottery from the region.
misuse.why: Vestige is a noun, not a verb; the museum 'preserves' or 'displays' pottery.

synonyms.vs: Trace is general and can be any small sign; vestige stresses something left over from a larger, earlier whole.
A remnant is a remaining piece, often physical; vestige often refers to customs, feelings or systems.
A relic is an object or custom from the past, often valued; vestige stresses how little remains.

origin: From Latin vestigium, 'footprint', the mark left by someone who has already gone.

definition: To mock someone or something, speaking of them as stupid or worthless.
nuance: Deride is formal and strongly critical, often used about critics, rivals or the public mocking an idea. It is very common in the passive: 'widely derided as unrealistic'. It is harsher than 'criticise' because it adds scorn and laughter.

examples.text: When the Impressionists first exhibited, critics derided their paintings as messy, unfinished sketches.
The plan was widely derided as unworkable when it was first announced last year.
Stop deriding his cooking; at least he tried.
She derides anyone who disagrees with her, which is why meetings with her are so tense.
Wegener's theory of continental drift was derided by many geologists for decades before it was finally accepted.
Members should not deride the contributions of colleagues during formal discussions.

cloze.text: Critics ___ the novel as silly when it first appeared, mocking it with open scorn, though it is now a classic.
Instead of debating his ideas seriously, his opponents ___ them, treating them with scornful laughter.
It is easy to ___ new technology, but many inventions once laughed at are now essential.

misuse.text: The audience derided the singer with a long, warm standing ovation.
misuse.why: Deride means to mock with contempt; a warm standing ovation shows admiration.

misuse.text: He derided from his original plan and took a different route.
misuse.why: Deride means to mock; the writer probably meant 'deviated' or 'departed'.

synonyms.vs: Mock is broader and can be playful; deride is always scornful and dismissive.
Ridicule focuses on making someone look foolish; deride adds contempt, often in public comment.
Scorn is a feeling or a refusal; deride is the act of expressing it, usually in words.

confusables.note: Derive means to get something from a source.

origin: From Latin deridere, 'to laugh at' or 'to laugh down'.

definition: The exact opposite of something, or a strong contrast between two ideas.
nuance: Antithesis is formal and common in essays, especially in 'the antithesis of', as in 'the antithesis of democracy'. In philosophy and rhetoric it also names the opposing idea in an argument, or a sentence built on balanced contrasts. The plural is 'antitheses'.

examples.text: Her calm, careful style is the antithesis of her brother's loud, impulsive approach.
Censorship, the author argues, is the antithesis of a free and open university.
Honestly, that meeting was the antithesis of productive: two hours and not one decision.
Romantic poets saw the smoky industrial city as the antithesis of the natural world they celebrated.
The minister said the new rules were the antithesis of what voters had been promised.
The essay explores the antitheses of light and dark that run through the whole poem.

cloze.text: Calm, shy and tidy, he was the ___ of the wild rock star his fans expected: the exact opposite in every way.
In dialectical argument, each thesis provokes its ___, and from the clash of the two a synthesis emerges.
Far from being similar, the two poems are opposites: the second is the very ___ of the first, dark where it is light.

misuse.text: The two sisters were an antithesis, alike in every single way.
misuse.why: Antithesis means the exact opposite, so it cannot describe things that are alike.

misuse.text: His opinion is antithesis to mine.
misuse.why: Antithesis is a noun used with 'the' and 'of': 'the antithesis of mine'. The adjective pattern is 'antithetical to'.

phrases: This approach is the very antithesis of...

synonyms.vs: Opposite is everyday and neutral; antithesis is formal and stresses a complete, often dramatic contrast.
A contrast is any noticeable difference; an antithesis is a direct opposite.
A contradiction is a statement or situation in conflict with itself or another; an antithesis is something entirely opposed.

origin: From Greek antithesis, 'a setting against', from anti, 'against', and tithenai, 'to place'.

sense: deny any connection with or responsibility for
definition: To say publicly that you have no connection with, support for or responsibility for something.
nuance: Disavow is formal and common in politics, law and journalism, when people or organisations distance themselves from statements, members or past views. It often hints at embarrassment or damage control. It is stronger and more public than simply 'deny'.

examples.text: After the offensive posts came to light, the party quickly disavowed the candidate and withdrew its support.
The scientist later disavowed her early research, admitting that the sample had been far too small.
The company disavows any responsibility for content posted by users on its forums.
I'm not disavowing what I said; I just worded it badly.
He spent the rest of his life trying to disavow the reckless young man he had been.
Many writers who had praised the revolution later disavowed it as its violence became clear.

cloze.text: The band publicly ___ the fan club, declaring they had no connection with it, after it began selling fake merchandise.
The candidate was urged to ___ the extreme group that had backed her and state publicly that she had no link with it.
Rather than ___ his earlier views, the philosopher explained how they had developed over time.

misuse.text: She disavowed her love for him in a long, passionate speech in front of everyone.
misuse.why: Disavow means to deny or reject; declaring love openly is 'avowing' or 'confessing' it.

misuse.text: The teacher disavowed the essay because it was handed in two days late.
misuse.why: Disavow means denying a connection with something; refusing late work is 'rejecting' it.

phrases: ...was quick to disavow any link with...

synonyms.vs: Renounce means formally giving up a belief, claim or title; disavow means denying any link or support.
Repudiate is stronger, rejecting something as false or unjust; disavow often distances oneself to avoid blame.
Disown is everyday and often personal, as with family; disavow is formal and public.
Deny is general and covers facts; disavow is about rejecting a connection or responsibility.

confusables.note: Disallow means to refuse to accept something as valid, such as a goal or a claim.

sense: the philosophical study of what exists
definition: The branch of philosophy that asks what exists and what kinds of things there are.
nuance: Ontology is a technical term in philosophy, and in the social sciences it also means a theory's assumptions about what is real, such as whether 'society' exists beyond individuals. It pairs with epistemology, which asks how we know things, and the two are often confused. In computing, an ontology is a structured set of categories.

examples.text: Ontology asks basic questions such as whether numbers, minds or societies really exist.
Before designing the study, students must state the ontology behind their research: what they believe is real.
Medieval philosophers built elaborate ontologies ranking everything from stones to angels.
Our seminar on ontology ended with everyone arguing about whether a hole is really a thing.
'Do I exist when nobody is watching?' asked the robot, who had become obsessed with ontology.
Applicants should explain how the ontology behind their research, their view of what is real, shapes the methods they propose.

cloze.text: While epistemology asks how we know things, ___ asks what things exist in the first place.
Within metaphysics, questions about which things really exist, such as numbers or minds, belong to ___.
Each research approach rests on an epistemology, about how we gain knowledge, and an ___, about what is real.

misuse.text: She is training in ontology so she can treat patients with cancer.
misuse.why: Ontology is the study of what exists; the branch of medicine that treats cancer is oncology.

misuse.text: Our ontology lecture explained how we can know whether historical sources are reliable.
misuse.why: How we know things is epistemology; ontology asks what exists.

phrases: The study adopts a realist ontology, assuming...
In terms of ontology, the author treats...

synonyms.vs: Metaphysics is the wider branch of philosophy about reality; ontology is the part of it concerned with what exists.
A worldview is a general outlook on life; an ontology is a precise account of what exists.

confusables.note: Oncology is the branch of medicine that deals with cancer.

origin: From modern Latin ontologia, coined by philosophers in the early 1600s from Greek on, ontos, 'being', and -logia, 'study'.

definition: An old, short saying that many people accept as true, such as 'practice makes perfect'.
nuance: Adage is used in writing to introduce or question a piece of traditional wisdom, as in 'the old adage that time is money'. It is neutral but often sets up a challenge: 'the adage may not hold'. 'Old adage' is very common, though some editors think it repeats itself.

examples.text: My grandmother lived by the adage that you should never go to bed angry.
The study tests the old adage that you get what you pay for, comparing cheap and expensive running shoes.
The familiar adage 'no news is good news' does not apply to medical test results.
Nervous investors were reminded of the adage that what goes up must come down.
Folk adages about the weather, such as 'red sky at night', are sometimes surprisingly accurate.
'Better late than never,' he muttered, recalling his father's favourite adage as he ran for the train.

cloze.text: As the old ___ goes, 'look before you leap', a saying worth remembering before you sign any contract.
The pairs solved the puzzle faster, supporting the old ___ that two heads are better than one: a saying science agrees with.
Every culture has its own ___, short traditional sayings passed down through generations.

misuse.text: In his speech, the president coined a bold new adage about the economy that nobody had heard before.
misuse.why: An adage is an old, well-known saying, so a brand-new remark cannot be one.

misuse.text: He wrote a long adage of three pages explaining his theory.
misuse.why: An adage is a short traditional saying, not a long piece of writing.

phrases: As the old adage has it, ...
The adage that... may no longer hold.

synonyms.vs: A proverb is a fixed traditional sentence of advice; adage stresses long-accepted truth and is used more in commentary.
A maxim is a rule for behaviour, often from one thinker; an adage is anonymous folk wisdom.
A cliché is any overused phrase and the word is critical; adage is neutral.

confusables.note: Adagio is a musical term for a slow tempo, or a slow piece.

origin: From French adage, from Latin adagium, 'a saying'.

sense: disrespectful of holy things; (of language) offensive, swearing
definition: Showing disrespect for God or holy things; of language, offensive and full of swearing.
nuance: Profane describes language, jokes or behaviour that offend religious feeling, and 'profane language' is a formal way of saying swearing. It is critical and sounds serious or old-fashioned. In religious studies and anthropology it can simply mean 'not sacred', as in 'the sacred and the profane', with no insult intended.

examples.text: The priest was shocked when the tourists made profane jokes inside the ancient chapel.
Medieval laws punished profane speech, such as cursing in God's name, with fines or public shame.
The study found that readers trusted online reviews less when they contained profane language.
The broadcaster apologised after a guest's profane language was aired before the watershed.
Visitors are asked to avoid profane or disrespectful behaviour within the cathedral grounds.
Grandad never swore, so even a mildly profane word from him made us all laugh.

cloze.text: The cathedral banned the band after they used ___ language during a concert in the nave.
Swearing in church was once a crime: such ___ words were seen as an insult to God himself.
The comedian's ___ jokes about saints and angels offended many religious viewers.

misuse.text: The choir sang a deeply profane hymn of praise at the Easter service.
misuse.why: Profane means disrespectful of holy things, so it cannot describe a hymn of praise.

misuse.text: He spoke so profane that the teacher sent him out of the room.
misuse.why: Profane is an adjective; after 'spoke' you need the adverb 'profanely', or say 'used profane language'.

synonyms.vs: Blasphemous is narrower and stronger, meaning insulting God directly; profane covers wider disrespect, including everyday swearing.
Irreverent is lighter and can be approving, as in playful humour; profane is more serious and offends.
Vulgar means crude or in poor taste generally; profane is tied to religion or swearing.

origin: From Latin profanus, 'outside the temple', meaning not holy.

definition: To bring a people or country under complete control, especially by force.
nuance: Subjugate is formal and strongly negative, used in history and politics about conquest, empire and oppression. It is also used about groups kept powerless within a society. It implies a lasting loss of freedom, not just one defeat.

examples.text: The empire used its armies to subjugate neighbouring kingdoms and force them to pay heavy taxes.
Historians have shown how colonial powers subjugated local populations through laws as well as violence.
In the novel, a cruel queen subjugates the mountain villages until a young shepherd leads a revolt.
The documentary shows how the invaders subjugated the island within a single summer.
The charter forbids any member state from subjugating another by force or economic pressure.
Honestly, the new kitten has completely subjugated the dog; he won't even go near his own bed.

cloze.text: The Romans did not simply defeat the tribes; they ___ them, ruling their lands for centuries.
No nation should be allowed to ___ another, forcing its people to live under foreign rule with no rights.
The invaders spent decades trying to ___ the mountain clans and keep them under permanent control, but they kept rebelling.

misuse.text: The kind teacher subjugated her pupils by giving them more freedom.
misuse.why: Subjugate means to force under control, which is the opposite of giving freedom.

misuse.text: My essay subjugates the history of trade unions in Wales.
misuse.why: Subjugate means to conquer or dominate; the writer probably meant 'is about' and confused it with 'subject'.

synonyms.vs: Conquer is about defeating and taking land; subjugate stresses keeping the defeated people under control afterwards.
Oppress means treating people cruelly and unfairly over time; subjugate focuses on bringing them under rule.
Subdue can be gentle or temporary, as with a fire or a crowd; subjugate means lasting domination.

origin: From Latin subjugare, 'to bring under the yoke'. Romans made defeated soldiers walk under a frame of spears shaped like a yoke.

definition: An indirect remark that hints at something bad or improper without saying it openly.
nuance: Innuendo is usually critical: it describes sly hints that damage a reputation, often in politics, gossip or court cases. In comedy it also means jokes with a hidden rude meaning. It is often uncountable, as in 'rumour and innuendo'.

examples.text: He never accused her directly, but his innuendo made everyone think she had stolen the money.
The candidate complained that the campaign against him relied on rumour and innuendo rather than facts.
The court ruled that the article's innuendo was defamatory, even though it made no false statement outright.
The study shows how Victorian novels conveyed scandal through innuendo, since direct description was not acceptable.
That old sitcom is full of innuendos my parents pretend not to understand.
Researchers found that innuendoes in online reviews damaged restaurants as much as open complaints did.

cloze.text: She never said he was lying; she relied on ___, raising an eyebrow every time he spoke.
The article made no direct accusations; it relied on rumour and ___ about the manager's private life.
Old seaside postcards are famous for their cheeky ___, with jokes that mean two things at once.

misuse.text: The report stated openly and clearly that the minister had lied, an innuendo nobody could miss.
misuse.why: Innuendo is an indirect hint; a clear, open statement is an accusation, not innuendo.

misuse.text: The music teacher praised her singing with a warm innuendo of encouragement.
misuse.why: Innuendo hints at something bad or improper; for a kind remark, use 'word' or 'note'.

phrases: Rather than offering evidence, the author relies on innuendo...
...a campaign built on rumour and innuendo

synonyms.vs: Insinuation is very close but usually a single sly suggestion; innuendo often describes a general style of hinting.
An implication is anything suggested and is neutral; innuendo is a hint that is unpleasant or improper.
An allusion is an indirect reference, often literary and harmless; innuendo carries a hidden negative meaning.

origin: Latin for 'by nodding at' or 'by hinting'. It was used in old legal documents to explain what a remark really meant.

sense: absolutely, without any doubt or exception
definition: In a direct, absolute way that allows no doubt or exception.
nuance: Categorically is common in official statements, especially with 'deny', 'reject' and 'state'. It shows total certainty, so in academic writing use it carefully: most evidence supports claims rather than proving them beyond question. It is the opposite of hedging.

examples.text: The minister categorically denied the claims, saying there was 'no truth whatsoever' in the report.
We cannot say categorically that the drug causes these side effects, since the sample was small.
I categorically refuse to watch that film again; once was more than enough.
The company categorically rejects any suggestion that it misled its customers.
'I was not there that night,' she said categorically, staring straight at the detective.
Few historians would state categorically that a single cause led to the First World War.

cloze.text: The club ___ denied the rumours: the manager was not leaving, full stop.
Careful scientists rarely state anything ___: they hedge, saying results 'suggest' rather than 'prove'.
The spokesperson stated ___, without any hedging or exceptions, that no data had been lost.

misuse.text: The results suggest, categorically but tentatively, that sleep may affect memory.
misuse.why: Categorically means with absolute certainty, so it contradicts 'suggest' and 'tentatively'.

misuse.text: The books were arranged categorically on the shelves, with history first and then science.
misuse.why: Categorically means absolutely, not 'by category'; say 'by subject' or 'into categories'.

phrases: It cannot be categorically stated that...

synonyms.vs: Absolutely is everyday and emphatic; categorically is formal and used for statements and denials.
Flatly suggests a blunt refusal or denial; categorically stresses that no exception is allowed.
Unequivocally means without any ambiguity; categorically means without any exception or condition.

definition: The fact of taking part in, or knowingly allowing, something wrong or illegal done by others.
nuance: Complicity is a serious, formal word used in law, ethics, history and journalism. It covers not only active help but also knowingly staying silent or looking away. It is usually followed by 'in', as in 'complicity in the fraud'.

examples.text: The bank manager denied any complicity in the fraud, insisting he had no idea his staff were stealing.
Historians continue to debate the complicity of ordinary citizens who stayed silent under the regime.
By laughing at his cruel jokes, we showed a kind of complicity, even if we didn't mean to.
The inquiry will examine whether officials showed complicity by ignoring repeated warnings.
She saw the guilty look on her sister's face and knew at once the extent of her complicity.
The paper examines how consumer demand creates complicity in poor working conditions abroad.

cloze.text: The guard's ___ in the escape was proved when investigators found he had left the gate unlocked on purpose.
Staying silent while a colleague is bullied can amount to ___ in the bullying.
The documents revealed the company's ___ in the cover-up: its directors knew and said nothing.

misuse.text: The complicity of the instructions made the new software hard to use.
misuse.why: Complicity means involvement in wrongdoing; the writer meant 'complexity'.

misuse.text: She was praised for her complicity in raising money for the local hospital.
misuse.why: Complicity is involvement in something wrong; for helping a good cause use 'involvement' or 'part'.

phrases: Silence can amount to complicity in...

synonyms.vs: Collusion is secret cooperation to cheat or deceive; complicity can include simply allowing wrongdoing.
Involvement is neutral and can be in anything; complicity is always involvement in something wrong.
Connivance means secretly allowing wrongdoing; complicity covers both helping and allowing.

confusables.note: Complexity means being complicated.
Complacency means being too satisfied to notice dangers or problems.

sense: dishonest and cunning in getting what you want
definition: Using clever, hidden and dishonest methods to get what you want.
nuance: Devious is critical and describes people, plans and methods that work through tricks rather than openly. It can be used half-admiringly for clever schemes in games or stories. In older or literary use it can also mean winding or indirect, as in 'a devious route'.

examples.text: The devious student copied her friend's homework, then changed a few words so the teacher wouldn't notice.
Investigators described the scam as one of the most devious they had seen, targeting elderly savers.
My little brother is so devious; he always gets me blamed for things he did.
The study suggests that children learn devious strategies, such as hiding toys, earlier than once thought.
Machiavelli advises the prince to use devious means when honest ones fail.
Any devious attempt to influence the judges will lead to immediate disqualification.

cloze.text: The ___ plan relied on hidden tricks and fake invoices rather than anything honest or open.
Don't trust him: he is charming on the surface but ___ underneath, always plotting something.
The villain's ___ scheme involved secretly swapping the real diamond for a glass copy.

misuse.text: She is so devious that she always tells you exactly what she thinks to your face.
misuse.why: Devious means sneaky and indirect, so open honesty is the opposite.

misuse.text: His opinions were devious from the rest of the group.
misuse.why: Devious means sneaky, not 'different from'; the writer probably meant 'deviated from' or 'differed from'.

synonyms.vs: Cunning stresses cleverness at tricking people and can be admiring; devious stresses dishonesty and hidden aims.
Sly is often small-scale and playful; devious suggests a more planned deception.
Deceitful is about lying directly; devious is about indirect, roundabout trickery.

confusables.note: Deviant means departing from what is socially normal or accepted.

origin: From Latin devius, 'off the road', so a devious person avoids the straight path.

sense: bringing strong images or memories to mind
definition: Bringing strong images, memories or feelings clearly into the mind.
nuance: Evocative is approving and common in reviews and literary criticism, describing writing, music, smells, photographs and places. It is often followed by 'of', as in 'evocative of childhood summers'. Unlike 'provocative', it does not suggest annoyance or challenge.

examples.text: The smell of the old bakery was so evocative that she suddenly felt seven years old again.
Critics praised the documentary's evocative footage of London in the 1960s.
Heaney's poems use evocative images of peat, farming and family life to explore Irish history.
That song is really evocative of our first holiday together.
The museum's new gallery uses evocative everyday objects to tell the story of migration.
The study found that street names evocative of nature made new housing estates seem more attractive.

cloze.text: The novel opens with an ___ description of a foggy harbour that brings back memories of every seaside town I knew as a child.
Old photographs are powerfully ___ of a world that no longer exists.
Her music is quietly ___, calling up memories of rainy afternoons and empty train stations.

misuse.text: His rude, evocative comments were meant to start a fight with the referee.
misuse.why: Evocative means bringing images or memories to mind; comments meant to annoy are 'provocative'.

misuse.text: The report was dry and evocative, with nothing but tables and figures.
misuse.why: Evocative writing brings images or feelings to mind, so it clashes with dry tables and figures.

synonyms.vs: Vivid means clear and lively in itself; evocative stresses calling up memories or feelings in the reader or viewer.
Reminiscent simply means reminding you of something; evocative suggests a stronger emotional effect.
Atmospheric creates a mood in the moment; evocative calls up something absent, such as the past.

confusables.note: Provocative means intended to cause anger, argument or a strong reaction.

origin: From Latin evocare, 'to call out' or 'to summon'.

sense: change of a poor area as wealthier people move in
definition: The process by which a poorer urban area changes as wealthier people move in, often pushing out existing residents.
nuance: Gentrification is a key term in sociology, geography and urban policy. It is often critical, stressing rising rents and the displacement of long-standing communities, though some writers also point to benefits such as investment and safer streets. It refers to a process over time, not a single building project.

examples.text: As cafes and galleries opened and rents doubled, long-time residents complained that gentrification was driving them out.
The sociologist Ruth Glass coined the term gentrification in 1964 to describe changes in working-class districts of London.
Researchers measured gentrification by tracking changes in rents, incomes and types of business over twenty years.
My old street has gone through serious gentrification; there's a shop that sells only sourdough now.
The council's plan aims to manage gentrification so that local families can afford to stay.
From her window she watched the gentrification of the neighbourhood, one renovated house at a time.

cloze.text: Rising rents and new wine bars are classic signs of ___, as wealthier newcomers transform a poorer district.
Critics of ___ point out that when richer newcomers move in, the original working-class residents rarely benefit.
The cheap artists' quarter fell victim to ___: the artists who made it fashionable could no longer afford it.

misuse.text: The gentrification of the village left it poorer, emptier and more run-down than ever.
misuse.why: Gentrification brings wealthier residents and investment; decline and decay are the opposite.

misuse.text: He went through a gentrification and now only wears designer suits.
misuse.why: Gentrification describes changes to an area or neighbourhood, not to a person's style.

phrases: The gentrification of... has led to...

synonyms.vs: Regeneration is usually a positive, planned improvement; gentrification focuses on who moves in and who is pushed out.
Urban renewal is official redevelopment, often by government; gentrification is often driven by private buyers and the market.

roots.meaning: people of high social class (Old French)

origin: Coined in 1964 by the sociologist Ruth Glass to describe middle-class 'gentry' moving into working-class districts of London.

definition: Continuing without stopping, usually in an annoying way.
nuance: Incessant is almost always used about unpleasant things such as noise, rain, complaints, questions or demands. It suggests irritation or exhaustion, so 'incessant joy' sounds odd. It is common in both literary writing and news reports.

examples.text: The incessant barking from next door kept me awake until three in the morning.
Incessant rain over the weekend caused flooding across much of Cumbria.
The researchers found that incessant notifications reduced students' ability to concentrate on reading.
She grew tired of his incessant questions and finally walked out of the room.
The committee received incessant requests for further information, which delayed its final decision.
Dickens portrays the incessant noise and smoke of the industrial city as a kind of torment.

cloze.text: The ___ hum of the fridge never paused for a moment, and it slowly drove her mad.
She could not concentrate because of the neighbours' ___ drilling, which went on all day without a single break.
The toddler's ___ 'why?' questions never stopped, even at bedtime, and his parents were exhausted.

misuse.text: The incessant applause lasted only two seconds before the hall fell silent.
misuse.why: Incessant means continuing without stopping, so it cannot describe something that lasted two seconds.

misuse.text: He incessant asked his parents for more money.
misuse.why: Incessant is an adjective; use the adverb 'incessantly', or say 'his incessant requests for money'.

phrases: The incessant pressure to... has led to...

synonyms.vs: Constant can be neutral or positive, as in constant support; incessant is usually annoying.
Continual means often repeated, with breaks; incessant suggests no break at all.
Relentless suggests determined force that will not ease, like pressure; incessant stresses that something never stops.

confusables.note: Insistent means firmly demanding that something happens.

origin: From Latin incessans, from in-, 'not', and cessare, 'to stop'.

definition: Interested only in your own group or country and having little contact with outside ideas.
nuance: Insular is critical when used about people, communities or attitudes, suggesting a narrow, inward-looking view. It is common in discussions of national politics, small towns, workplaces and academic fields. Its literal sense, 'of an island', survives in geography and history.

examples.text: The village was so insular that anyone who had lived there less than twenty years was called a newcomer.
Critics say the club's insular culture made it slow to spot talented players from abroad.
The author argues that the field became insular, citing its own journals and ignoring neighbouring disciplines.
Our office is pretty insular; nobody ever talks to the team on the other floor.
The review warned that an insular approach to recruitment would limit the range of views in the organisation.
Some historians link insular attitudes in Britain to its long history as an island nation.

cloze.text: The valley community was so ___ that it distrusted outsiders and showed no interest in the wider world.
The party was accused of being ___, more interested in its own members than in the wider public.
Travel can cure ___ thinking by showing people how differently others live.

misuse.text: She is very insular and loves meeting people from different cultures.
misuse.why: Insular means inward-looking and uninterested in outsiders, which contradicts loving other cultures.

misuse.text: Wear an insular jacket because it will be freezing tonight.
misuse.why: Insular means narrow in outlook; a jacket that keeps you warm is 'insulated'.

synonyms.vs: Parochial stresses concern only with local matters; insular stresses being cut off from outside contact.
Narrow-minded is everyday and about intolerance; insular is about isolation from other people and ideas.
Provincial suggests unsophisticated small-town ways; insular can describe a closed group of any size.

confusables.note: Insulated means protected from heat, cold, sound or electricity.

origin: From Latin insula, 'island', so insular people live as if on an island, cut off from others.

definition: So great or difficult that it cannot be dealt with or overcome.
nuance: Insurmountable is used about problems, obstacles, odds and differences, and is common in news, business and history. It is often paired with 'seemingly' or 'almost' to suggest that something looked impossible but was not. Avoid it for small difficulties: it sounds dramatic.

examples.text: With his team losing five-nil at half-time, the gap looked insurmountable.
The historian concludes that the monarchy's debts had become insurmountable by the 1780s.
What seemed like insurmountable obstacles to the project were solved within a few weeks.
Honestly, a pile of washing is not an insurmountable problem; just put the machine on.
Between the two brothers lay an insurmountable wall of old grudges.
The study found that language barriers, though serious, were rarely insurmountable for migrant students.

cloze.text: Despite seemingly ___ odds, the tiny charity raised enough money to rebuild the school.
The engineers declared the problem ___: no amount of money or time could fix it.
Their differences were not ___, and with patience the two sides reached an agreement.

misuse.text: The hill was so insurmountable that we reached the top in an hour.
misuse.why: Insurmountable means impossible to overcome, so reaching the top easily contradicts it.

misuse.text: She has an insurmountable collection of stamps from all over the world.
misuse.why: Insurmountable means impossible to overcome, not very large; for a huge collection use 'enormous' or 'vast'.

phrases: These difficulties, while serious, are not insurmountable.

synonyms.vs: Insuperable has the same meaning but is more formal and much rarer.
Overwhelming means too great to cope with; insurmountable means impossible to get past or solve.
Impossible is broader; insurmountable is specifically about obstacles that cannot be overcome.

roots.meaning: to climb (French, from Latin mons, mountain)

sense: the most perfect or typical example
definition: Being the most typical or perfect example of a particular kind of thing.
nuance: Quintessential is approving or neutral and is common in reviews, travel writing and cultural commentary. It says that something sums up a type completely, as in 'the quintessential English village'. It is easily overused, so save it for a genuinely typical case.

examples.text: With its thatched cottages, village green and old pub, it is the quintessential English village.
Fish and chips eaten on a windy pier is my idea of the quintessential British holiday.
Darwin's notebook sketch of a branching tree has become the quintessential image of evolution.
Reviewers called the film a quintessential coming-of-age story, full of first love and awkward parties.
Many critics regard Austen's Emma as the quintessential novel of manners.
He looked like the quintessential detective, complete with raincoat, notebook and tired eyes.

cloze.text: With his flat cap, tweed jacket and muddy spaniel, he was the ___ country gentleman: no purer example could exist.
For many fans, this album is the ___ nineties record, the one that sums up the very essence of the decade's pop.
To many visitors, afternoon tea with scones and jam is the ___ English custom, the most perfect example of Englishness there is.

misuse.text: The village is quintessential, nothing like any other village in England.
misuse.why: Quintessential means the most typical example, so it cannot describe something unlike all the others.

misuse.text: She quintessential agreed with everything he said.
misuse.why: Quintessential is an adjective meaning perfectly typical; it is not an adverb meaning 'completely'.

synonyms.vs: Typical just means normal for its kind; quintessential means the purest, most perfect example.
Archetypal suggests an original model that others copy; quintessential stresses being the best example.
Classic is everyday and broader, and can also mean of lasting quality.

origin: From medieval Latin quinta essentia, 'fifth essence': a fifth element, purer than earth, air, fire and water, thought to make up the heavens.

sense: guess or conclude from limited evidence
definition: To guess that something is true using the limited evidence you have.
nuance: Surmise is formal and slightly literary, common in detective fiction, history and careful academic writing. It admits that a conclusion is a reasonable guess, not proof. It is usually followed by 'that' or used in phrases such as 'as one might surmise'.

examples.text: From the mud on his boots, the detective surmised that he had walked across the fields.
We can only surmise what the cave paintings meant to the people who made them.
Given the empty fridge, I surmise that someone had a party while we were away.
Analysts surmised that the sudden sale of shares meant the company was in trouble.
The author surmises that the letter was written in haste, since it has no date or signature.
Without further data, the committee refrained from surmising the causes of the decline.

cloze.text: Historians can only ___ why the king changed his mind; with no records surviving, any answer is an educated guess.
From her tired face and wet coat, he ___ that she had walked all the way home, though it was only a guess.
Lacking direct evidence, the researchers could only tentatively ___ that the stone tools were used for cutting meat.

misuse.text: The experiment surmised beyond doubt that the drug was effective.
misuse.why: To surmise is to guess from limited evidence, so it cannot go with 'beyond doubt'; results 'proved' or 'showed' this.

misuse.text: She surmised all her friends to a party at her house.
misuse.why: Surmise means to guess, not to invite or call people together; perhaps 'summoned' was meant.

phrases: It is reasonable to surmise that...

synonyms.vs: Infer means reaching a logical conclusion from evidence; surmise admits the evidence is thin.
Speculate means forming theories without firm evidence, often at length; surmise is one quiet guess.
Conjecture is very close but more formal, and is often used as a noun.
Deduce means reasoning firmly from facts; surmise is much more tentative.

definition: So morally wrong or disgusting that people feel strong hatred for it.
nuance: Abhorrent is very strong and formal, used about cruelty, injustice, crimes and ideas that cause moral disgust. It is often followed by 'to', as in 'the idea was abhorrent to her'. Using it for small annoyances sounds exaggerated.

examples.text: Most people find cruelty to children abhorrent and want those responsible punished.
The judge called the attack on the elderly couple abhorrent and gave the maximum sentence.
The idea of eating meat became abhorrent to him after he spent a summer working on a farm.
Slavery, once defended by many politicians, is now universally regarded as abhorrent.
Honestly, pineapple on pizza isn't abhorrent; it's just a different taste.
Philosophers ask why some acts feel abhorrent to almost everyone, even when they cause no measurable harm.

cloze.text: Torture is ___ to any decent person: it violates the most basic human rights.
She found the idea of lying to her patients morally ___, so deeply wrong that she refused to take part.
The charity condemned the cruelty to the animals as ___, saying it filled its staff with moral disgust.

misuse.text: The cake was abhorrent, so everyone asked for a second slice.
misuse.why: Abhorrent means hateful or disgusting, so it clashes with everyone wanting more.

misuse.text: He abhorrent the idea of moving abroad.
misuse.why: Abhorrent is an adjective; the verb is 'abhor', as in 'he abhorred the idea'.

phrases: The practice is morally abhorrent because...

synonyms.vs: Repugnant is very close but often about things that offend taste as well as morals.
Offensive is much milder and can mean merely rude; abhorrent expresses deep moral disgust.
Detestable is about intense dislike; abhorrent adds a sense of moral horror.

origin: From Latin abhorrere, 'to shrink back from in horror', from ab, 'away', and horrere, 'to bristle'.

sense: mercy shown in punishing an offender
definition: The showing of mercy to an offender, especially by reducing or cancelling their punishment.
nuance: Clemency is used mainly in law and politics, about judges, presidents or monarchs who reduce or cancel a punishment. It is neutral to approving and often appears in 'appeal for clemency' and 'grant clemency'. It is uncountable, so do not say 'a clemency'.

examples.text: The judge showed clemency and gave the teenager community service instead of a prison sentence.
Roman emperors often used public acts of clemency towards defeated enemies to win popular support.
His lawyers have filed a final appeal for clemency with the state governor.
Moved by her plea, the king granted clemency to the rebels who had laid down their arms.
I'm begging for clemency here: I know the essay is late, but my laptop died.
The committee may recommend clemency where there is clear evidence of genuine remorse.

cloze.text: Under the constitution, only the governor can grant executive ___, so the prisoner's lawyers sent their final appeal to her.
At the ___ hearing, the prisoner's family asked the board to recommend that his life sentence be reduced.
The judge had already shown some leniency at sentencing, so his only remaining hope was presidential ___.

misuse.text: The judge showed great clemency by doubling the prisoner's sentence.
misuse.why: Clemency means making a punishment lighter, not harsher.

misuse.text: She thanked her friend for his clemency in lending her his lecture notes.
misuse.why: Clemency is mercy towards someone who has done wrong, not ordinary kindness or generosity.

phrases: ...appealed to the court for clemency on the grounds that...

synonyms.vs: Mercy is everyday and broad; clemency is formal and usually means an official decision to lessen a punishment.
Leniency is a general softness in judging or punishing; clemency is often a single act of mercy by someone in authority.
A pardon cancels a punishment completely; clemency can also mean simply reducing it.

origin: From Latin clementia, 'mildness, mercy', from clemens, 'mild'.

sense: able to be noticed or detected
definition: Able to be seen, heard or noticed, though sometimes only just.
nuance: Discernible is formal and very common in research writing about results, trends and patterns. It is often used with 'no' or 'barely' to say that something cannot be detected: 'no discernible effect'. It suggests some effort to notice, so it often describes small or faint things.

examples.text: Through the thick fog, the outline of the lighthouse was barely discernible.
The trial found no discernible effect of the supplement on memory or concentration.
There has been a discernible shift in public attitudes to working from home.
Is there any discernible difference between these two paint colours, or is it just me?
The auditors found no discernible pattern in the missing payments.
A discernible theme of loss runs through all of the poet's later work.

cloze.text: Statisticians searched the figures for a trend, but there was no ___ pattern: nothing they could pick out from the random noise.
Blind tasters found no ___ difference between the cheap coffee and the expensive one: they simply could not tell them apart.
After a year abroad, the change in her accent was barely ___: only her oldest friends could make it out.

misuse.text: She could discernible a faint light in the distance.
misuse.why: Discernible is an adjective; the verb is discern: 'she could discern a faint light'.

misuse.text: Her discernible taste in wine impressed the waiter.
misuse.why: Discernible means able to be noticed; for good judgement or taste the word is 'discerning'.

phrases: There is no discernible evidence that...

synonyms.vs: Perceptible stresses what the senses can pick up; discernible is common for effects and patterns found by careful analysis.
Noticeable is everyday and suggests something fairly easy to see.
Detectable suggests measuring with instruments or tests; discernible suggests the eye or mind picking something out.

confusables.note: Discerning describes a person with good judgement or taste.

origin: From Latin discernere, 'to separate' or 'to tell apart'.

definition: Extremely happy and excited, usually because of a success or good news.
nuance: Elated describes a strong burst of joy, usually after a particular event such as a win, a result or good news. It is stronger than pleased and describes a passing mood, not a personality. People are elated at, about or by something.

examples.text: When she opened the letter and saw she had a place at medical school, she was elated.
Elated fans poured onto the pitch after the last-minute winner.
Participants who won small prizes reported feeling elated, but the effect had faded within an hour.
I was elated when the examiner said I'd passed, then terrified when I had to drive home alone.
The governors were elated by the inspection report, which rated the school outstanding for the first time.
He walked out of the exam hall elated, sure that he had answered every question well.

cloze.text: After months of anxious waiting, she was ___ at the news that the job was hers, so happy she felt lifted off her feet.
The ___ team lifted the trophy and danced and sang in the pouring rain.
He felt ___ at first, but the joy faded once he saw the size of the tax bill.

misuse.text: He felt elated after failing his driving test for the third time.
misuse.why: Elated means very happy, which does not fit failing a test.

misuse.text: The elated news spread quickly through the village.
misuse.why: Elated describes how people feel, not the news itself; say 'the joyful news' or 'the good news'.

synonyms.vs: Overjoyed is everyday and very close; elated is slightly more formal and suggests a lift in spirits.
Jubilant suggests open, often public celebration; elated is more about the inner feeling.
Ecstatic is even stronger and can sound overexcited or informal.

origin: From Latin elatus, 'lifted up', so an elated person feels raised up by joy.

definition: Therefore; used to introduce a conclusion that follows from what has just been said.
nuance: Ergo is the Latin for 'therefore' and links a premise to a conclusion. In logic and philosophy it is neutral, but in everyday speech it often sounds playful, ironic or a little showy. In essays, 'therefore' or 'thus' is usually the safer choice.

examples.text: The shop shuts at six and it's already ten past; ergo, no milk until tomorrow.
The premises are true and the argument is valid; ergo, the conclusion must also be true.
The minister insisted that the economy had grown and that, ergo, the policy had worked.
He had never lost a game of chess to a child; ergo, he assumed, he would not lose today.
The contract has expired and has not been renewed; ergo, neither party has any further obligation.
Some students reason that the reading is not assessed, ergo it is not worth doing.

cloze.text: Showing off his school Latin, he laid out his case like a philosopher: 'I cooked; ___, you wash up.'
With mock solemnity, she summed up the advert's flimsy logic: 'A celebrity wears these trainers; ___, you need them too.'
He reasoned in short, clipped, mock-formal steps: 'No ticket, no entry; ___, no concert for us tonight.'

misuse.text: Ergo the rain, we stayed indoors all afternoon.
misuse.why: Ergo introduces a conclusion and cannot mean 'because of'; say 'Because of the rain' instead.

misuse.text: She studied hard for weeks, ergo she failed the exam.
misuse.why: Ergo means therefore, so the second part must follow from the first; failing does not follow from hard study.

synonyms.vs: Therefore is the standard formal choice; ergo can sound showy or ironic in an essay.
Hence is common before a short noun phrase, as in 'hence the delay'; ergo sounds more like a step in logic.
Thus can also mean 'in this way'; ergo only marks a conclusion.

origin: Borrowed unchanged from Latin ergo, 'therefore'. It is best known from Descartes' phrase 'cogito, ergo sum', 'I think, therefore I am'.

sense: full of lively energy and cheerfulness
definition: Full of energy, excitement and cheerfulness, often in a lively, unrestrained way.
nuance: Exuberant is usually approving and describes people, moods, performances or styles bursting with life. It can also describe richly decorated art or plants growing thickly. Unlike elated, which is a feeling after good news, exuberant is about energy that shows on the outside.

examples.text: The exuberant puppy raced around the garden, barking and leaping at every butterfly.
The crowd gave an exuberant welcome to the team's open-top bus.
Baroque churches are known for their exuberant decoration, with gold leaf covering almost every surface.
My niece is so exuberant that she narrates everything she does at full volume.
The head teacher praised the pupils' exuberant performance at the school's centenary celebrations.
In the young novelist's letters, an exuberant style gives way to a quieter tone after the war.

cloze.text: The ___ toddler laughed, clapped and ran in circles, full of boundless energy.
Unlike his reserved brother, Tom was ___ at every party, overflowing with cheerful energy and high spirits.
His ___ dancing, all leaps and wild spins, made the whole room smile.

misuse.text: The exuberant library was silent apart from the ticking of a clock.
misuse.why: Exuberant means full of lively energy, which does not fit a silent room.

misuse.text: The exuberant price of the tickets put many fans off.
misuse.why: Exuberant means lively and joyful; for prices that are far too high, use 'exorbitant'.

phrases: The exuberant tone of... contrasts with...

synonyms.vs: Ebullient is more formal and suggests bubbling cheerfulness, especially in talk and manner.
Enthusiastic means keen on something; exuberant is about overflowing energy and high spirits.
Boisterous is noisy and rough, sometimes annoyingly so; exuberant is usually approving.

confusables.note: Exorbitant means far too expensive.

origin: From Latin exuberare, 'to be abundantly fruitful', from uber, 'fertile'.

sense: showily grand or far too ambitious
definition: Trying to seem very impressive or important, often far more than is realistic or needed.
nuance: Grandiose is almost always critical. It describes plans, buildings, claims or language that are too ambitious or showy to be taken seriously. In psychology it also describes an inflated sense of one's own importance.

examples.text: He announced grandiose plans to open a chain of hotels, but he couldn't even pay his rent.
The council scrapped its grandiose scheme for a new stadium after the costs tripled.
The architect's grandiose design was rejected as far too expensive for a village library.
Victorian railway stations were often grandiose, built to resemble cathedrals or palaces.
Psychologists distinguish grandiose narcissism, marked by confidence and dominance, from a more vulnerable form.
Stop making grandiose promises about getting fit and just go for a walk.

cloze.text: Critics dismissed the mayor's ___ vision of a skyline of gleaming towers as showy, self-important and wildly unrealistic.
Her essay was full of inflated, ___ claims about single-handedly changing the world, but offered very little evidence.
The plans were absurdly ___: a marble fountain, three towers and a private zoo for a tiny company.

misuse.text: The tiny, modest cottage was grandiose in its simplicity.
misuse.why: Grandiose means showily grand, so it contradicts tiny, modest and simple.

misuse.text: She made a grandiose donation that helped the charity enormously.
misuse.why: Grandiose is critical and means showy or overambitious; for a large, kind gift use 'generous' or 'substantial'.

synonyms.vs: Pompous describes self-important people and speech; grandiose more often describes plans, buildings and claims.
Ambitious can be approving; grandiose implies the ambition is unrealistic or showy.
Pretentious means pretending to be more cultured or important than you are; grandiose stresses size and scale.

confusables.note: Grandiloquent describes pompous, flowery language only.

origin: From French grandiose, from Italian grandioso, from Latin grandis, 'great'.

sense: bored or weary from having too much
definition: Tired, bored or no longer enthusiastic, after having had too much of something.
nuance: Jaded describes people, or their tastes, dulled by too much experience of something, such as travel, rich food or politics. It often carries a hint of cynicism. It is mildly critical or sympathetic and is common in journalism and reviews.

examples.text: After twenty years of reviewing films, she felt jaded: nothing on screen surprised or excited her any more.
Even jaded commuters looked up from their phones when a brass band started playing on the platform.
Many voters in the survey described themselves as jaded by years of constant campaigning.
I used to love theme parks, but I'm a bit jaded now; the queues ruin it.
The novel's narrator is a jaded diplomat whose cynicism slowly gives way to hope.
Organisers hope the new format will win back jaded visitors who stopped attending the fair.

cloze.text: After too many luxury holidays, he had become ___: even perfect beaches bored him.
The ___ old journalist rolled her eyes; she had heard every excuse a hundred times before.
Years of scandals have left many readers ___ and cynical, unable to feel shocked by anything.

misuse.text: The jaded toddler was thrilled by every new toy.
misuse.why: Jaded means bored from too much experience, the opposite of being thrilled by new things.

misuse.text: She wore a beautiful jaded necklace to the party.
misuse.why: Jaded means weary or cynical; a necklace made of the green stone is a 'jade necklace'.

synonyms.vs: Weary means tired in general; jaded means bored or dulled by having too much of something.
Cynical means distrusting people's motives; jaded is the worn-out feeling that often leads there.
World-weary suggests tiredness with life in general; jaded is often about one thing you have had too much of.

confusables.note: Jade is a green stone; it has nothing to do with jaded in meaning.

origin: From jade, an old word for a tired, worn-out horse, so a jaded person is worn out by too much.

definition: The people of future generations, especially as those who will remember or judge what we do.
nuance: Posterity is formal and a little grand, used about legacy, history and reputation. It appears in fixed phrases such as 'for posterity' (kept for the future) and 'posterity will judge'. It takes no plural and usually no article.

examples.text: We filmed my grandmother telling stories about her childhood so they would be kept for posterity.
Thousands of wartime letters have been preserved for posterity by a small local archive.
Renaissance patrons commissioned portraits partly to secure their reputation with posterity.
The old captain believed that posterity would forgive him, even if his crew never did.
Minutes must be recorded accurately, both for legal reasons and for posterity.
Hold that pose: I want to capture this moment for posterity!

cloze.text: Great leaders often worry about how ___, the generations still to come, will remember them.
The ancient library was built to preserve knowledge for ___: for readers centuries in the future.
The time capsule, to be opened in a hundred years, was the school's message to ___.

misuse.text: The ancient Romans were the posterity of modern Italians.
misuse.why: Posterity means the people who come after; the Romans came before, so they are ancestors.

misuse.text: The new factory brought great posterity to the town.
misuse.why: Posterity means future generations; for wealth and success the word is 'prosperity'.

synonyms.vs: Descendants are the children and later family of particular people; posterity means future generations in general.
Future generations is the plain modern phrase; posterity sounds grander and more formal.

confusables.note: Prosperity means wealth and success.

origin: From Latin posteritas, from posterus, 'coming after'.

definition: So wrong or bad that it deserves strong criticism and blame.
nuance: Reprehensible is a strong, formal word for behaviour that is morally wrong. It is used about actions, conduct and attitudes more than about people directly. It is common in official statements, legal judgments and editorials.

examples.text: Stealing money from a children's charity is reprehensible, and the court gave him a long sentence.
The inquiry described the company's treatment of whistle-blowers as morally reprehensible.
Some philosophers argue that lying is reprehensible even when it prevents harm.
Eating the last slice of cake without asking is frankly reprehensible behaviour.
The club condemned the reprehensible abuse aimed at the referee after the match.
She knew that reading her sister's diary was reprehensible, but curiosity won.

cloze.text: Bullying a new employee until she resigns is ___ conduct: it deserves to be condemned, not quietly excused.
The judge called the fraud, which targeted elderly victims, utterly ___ and morally indefensible.
Cheating his own friends was not just a mistake but deeply ___, and he deserved every bit of the blame he received.

misuse.text: Her reprehensible courage in rescuing the stranded climbers earned her a medal.
misuse.why: Reprehensible means deserving blame, so it cannot describe brave, praiseworthy actions.

misuse.text: The reprehensible weather ruined our picnic.
misuse.why: Reprehensible is a moral judgement on what people do; weather cannot deserve blame, so say 'awful'.

phrases: Such conduct is morally reprehensible because...
However reprehensible..., it does not follow that...

synonyms.vs: Deplorable can describe bad conditions as well as conduct; reprehensible is specifically about blameworthy behaviour.
Contemptible adds personal scorn for the person who did wrong.
Blameworthy is milder and more technical, common in ethics and law.

origin: From Latin reprehendere, 'to hold back' or 'to rebuke', from prehendere, 'to seize'.

definition: Extremely harsh and critical, often in a way meant to hurt or embarrass.
nuance: Scathing describes criticism, reviews, reports and remarks that attack without mercy. It is very common in journalism, especially 'a scathing report' and 'scathing about'. It describes words and looks, not physical attacks.

examples.text: The critic's scathing review called the film 'two hours of my life I will never get back'.
A scathing report into the hospital found failures at every level of management.
Orwell was scathing about writers who hid weak ideas behind long, vague words.
My sister was scathing about my haircut, so I'm wearing a hat for a week.
The auditors delivered a scathing assessment of the council's spending controls.
She gave him a scathing look and left the room without a word.

cloze.text: The inspectors' ___ report condemned almost every aspect of how the prison was run.
Reviewers were ___ about the sequel, calling it lazy, dull and far too long.
He expected gentle feedback but got a ___ attack on every paragraph of his thesis.

misuse.text: The teacher wrote a scathing comment praising my excellent essay.
misuse.why: Scathing means harshly critical, so it cannot describe praise.

misuse.text: The scathing sun burned our shoulders at the beach.
misuse.why: Scathing describes harsh words and criticism; for intense heat use 'scorching'.

phrases: In a scathing critique of..., the author argues...

synonyms.vs: Withering suggests making someone feel small, often with a look or a short remark.
Caustic stresses sarcastic, biting humour; scathing stresses how severe the criticism is.
Damning means showing clearly that someone is guilty or wrong; scathing is about the harshness of the tone.

origin: From the old verb scathe, 'to harm', which survives today in unscathed.

sense: treat a person or group as shameful
definition: To treat a person, group or condition as shameful or unworthy, usually unfairly.
nuance: Stigmatise is used about society treating people, illnesses or behaviours as shameful. It is common in social science, health and policy writing, and nearly always implies that the treatment is unfair. The noun stigma is even more frequent.

examples.text: In the past, people with epilepsy were often stigmatised, avoided by neighbours and refused work.
Campaigners say the new rules stigmatise families who rely on food banks.
Careless headlines risk stigmatising people who are already struggling with their mental health.
The study examines how tabloid coverage stigmatises young people from certain neighbourhoods.
Come on, don't stigmatise him just because he failed one exam.
In the village, the young widow was stigmatised for remarrying within a year.

cloze.text: Calling the illness 'shameful' only serves to ___ patients and discourage them from seeking treatment.
For decades, society ___ unmarried mothers, treating them as a disgrace to their families.
Health workers feared that naming patients publicly would ___ them, branding them as careless or dirty.

misuse.text: The award stigmatised her as one of the country's finest young scientists.
misuse.why: Stigmatise means mark as shameful; for public praise or recognition, use 'recognised' or 'celebrated'.

misuse.text: Many people stigmatise of mental illness without realising it.
misuse.why: Stigmatise takes a direct object with no 'of': people stigmatise mental illness.

synonyms.vs: Brand means label someone harshly, often publicly; stigmatise suggests lasting social shame.
Marginalise means push a group to the edge of society; stigmatise is about attaching shame to them.
Demonise is stronger, portraying people as evil or dangerous.

origin: From Greek stigma, a mark made by a pointed tool, such as the brand once burned onto slaves or criminals.

sense: make something clear by explaining it
definition: To make something clear by explaining it in more detail.
nuance: Elucidate is formal and academic, used about explaining ideas, mechanisms, causes or meanings. It suggests shedding light on something that was obscure. In speech it can sound stiff, and asking someone to 'elucidate' can sound sarcastic.

examples.text: The tutor drew a simple diagram to elucidate the idea, and suddenly the whole class understood.
Scientists say they have finally elucidated how the virus enters human cells.
The appendix elucidates the methods used to collect and clean the data.
Could you elucidate? I have no idea what 'synergistic leverage' is supposed to mean.
In elucidating the causes of the revolution, the author draws on hundreds of local records.
He elucidated his theory at great length, though nobody in the carriage had asked.

cloze.text: The lecturer's examples helped to ___ the theory, shedding light on what had seemed obscure.
Further research is needed to ___ the exact mechanism, which remains poorly understood.
In a long footnote, the editor ___ the poem's references to Greek myth, making them clear to modern readers.

misuse.text: The rising sun elucidated the room with golden light.
misuse.why: Elucidate means make an idea clear by explaining it, not light up a place; use 'lit up' or 'illuminated'.

misuse.text: She elucidated me about the rules of the game.
misuse.why: You elucidate something, not someone: 'she elucidated the rules for me'.

phrases: Further work is needed to elucidate...

synonyms.vs: Clarify is more common and often means removing confusion; elucidate suggests a fuller, deeper explanation.
Explain is everyday; elucidate is formal and academic.
Illuminate is more literary and suggests revealing new understanding rather than explaining step by step.

origin: From Latin elucidare, 'to make light', from lucidus, 'bright, clear'.

definition: To criticise someone or something unfairly, making them seem less important or worthy.
nuance: Denigrate is formal and suggests unfair or dismissive criticism, aimed at reputations, achievements or groups. It is common in arguments about respect and bias. Saying that someone denigrates something is itself a criticism of them.

examples.text: Instead of praising her hard work, her boss denigrated it, calling the report 'basic and amateurish'.
Early critics tended to denigrate the Impressionists, dismissing their paintings as unfinished sketches.
The coach was fined for publicly denigrating the referees after the final.
You always denigrate your own work, and honestly it's really good.
The code prohibits any advertising that denigrates a competitor's products.
Historians have warned against denigrating oral history as less reliable than written records.

cloze.text: This is not to ___ the work of volunteers: without them, the festival could not run at all.
It is unfair to ___ the achievements of earlier scientists, running them down simply because they lacked modern equipment.
In his memoir he repeatedly ___ his former colleagues, unfairly belittling their talent to make himself look better.

misuse.text: The judges denigrated her performance with the top prize and a standing ovation.
misuse.why: Denigrate means criticise unfairly, not honour or reward.

misuse.text: The old paintwork had denigrated badly after years of rain.
misuse.why: Denigrate is about unfair criticism; for things wearing away, use 'deteriorated' or 'degraded'.

phrases: This is not to denigrate..., but...

synonyms.vs: Belittle means make something seem small or unimportant; denigrate stresses an unfair attack on worth or reputation.
Disparage is very close but slightly milder, often subtle or casual.
Defame is a legal idea: harming a reputation with false statements.

sense: a short, vivid description of a scene
definition: A short piece of writing, film or description that captures one scene, moment or character.
nuance: Vignette is used in literature, film, journalism and research for a brief, vivid sketch rather than a full story. In social science, vignettes are short imagined scenarios that participants react to. It is neutral and often approving.

examples.text: The book is not one continuous story but a series of vignettes, each a short glimpse of village life.
The documentary opens with a vignette of a fisherman mending his nets at dawn.
Participants read short vignettes describing workplace conflicts and rated how fair each response seemed.
Her speech included a touching vignette about her first day as a nurse.
Grandad's stories are lovely little vignettes, but they never seem to have an ending.
Each chapter closes with a quiet vignette: a cup of tea cooling, a door left open.

cloze.text: Instead of a full plot, the film offers brief ___, short glimpses into the lives of strangers in one city.
Her travel column is a lively ___ of market life, capturing the noise and smells in three short paragraphs.
In the experiment, each volunteer read a ___, a short imagined scenario, and said how they would respond.

misuse.text: The novelist spent ten years on her vignette, a thousand-page family saga.
misuse.why: A vignette is short by definition, so a thousand-page saga is the opposite.

misuse.text: The article ends with a brief vignette: a table of last year's sales figures.
misuse.why: A vignette is a short descriptive scene or sketch, not a table of figures or data.

phrases: Participants were presented with a vignette in which...

synonyms.vs: A sketch can be any brief outline or comic scene; a vignette is usually a vivid, carefully observed moment.
An anecdote is a short, often amusing story with a point; a vignette is a descriptive snapshot, often without one.
A scene is usually part of a larger work; a vignette often stands alone.

origin: From French vignette, 'little vine', first used for the vine-leaf decorations printed around pages in books.

sense: take away the right to vote or a voice
definition: To take away someone's right to vote, or to leave them without a voice or power in society.
nuance: Disenfranchise is used in politics, law and history, first about voting rights and more broadly about groups who feel shut out. The form 'disenfranchised' is common as an adjective. It is serious and usually critical of whoever is doing it.

examples.text: Strict property rules disenfranchised most working men in early nineteenth-century Britain, leaving voting to a wealthy minority.
Campaigners warn that closing rural polling stations could disenfranchise elderly voters.
Honestly, I feel completely disenfranchised; the student council never asks what we think.
Any system that disenfranchises citizens through administrative error must be reviewed urgently.
The islanders felt that each new rule from the distant capital was slowly disenfranchising them.
Historians have shown how literacy tests were used to disenfranchise voters in parts of the American South.

cloze.text: Before women won the vote, the law effectively ___ half the adult population, denying them any say at the ballot box.
A computer error threatened to ___ thousands of voters by deleting their names from the electoral register.
Holding the ballot only online risked ___ older members without internet access, who would lose their vote.

misuse.text: The election disenfranchised a record number of new voters by welcoming them to the polls.
misuse.why: Disenfranchise means take away the right to vote, the opposite of welcoming new voters.

misuse.text: The government disenfranchised the vote from the island's residents.
misuse.why: You disenfranchise people, not the vote: say 'disenfranchised the residents' or 'took the vote away from them'.

synonyms.vs: Marginalise means push to the edge of society; disenfranchise specifically removes votes, rights or a say.
Exclude is general; disenfranchise is about political or civic power.
Disempower is broader and covers any loss of control or confidence.

origin: Built from enfranchise, 'to set free' or give rights, from Old French franc, 'free'.

sense: a mild word used in place of a harsh one
definition: A mild or indirect word or phrase used in place of one that seems too harsh or embarrassing.
nuance: Euphemism covers polite softenings in everyday speech and deliberate spin in politics and business. In analysis it is often critical, suggesting language that hides an unpleasant truth. 'A euphemism for' is the usual pattern.

examples.text: Saying someone is 'between jobs' is a polite euphemism for saying they are unemployed.
Orwell argued that political euphemisms make harsh actions sound harmless.
The company called the job cuts 'a restructuring', a euphemism that fooled nobody.
The style guide asks writers to avoid euphemisms and to state risks plainly.
'Compact and bijou,' read the advert, a euphemism the couple soon learned meant tiny.
Linguists study how euphemisms for taboo subjects wear out and are replaced over time.

cloze.text: 'Pre-loved' is just a polite ___ for second-hand, used to make old clothes sound appealing.
The memo was full of soft-sounding ___ like 'right-sizing' and 'efficiency savings', all meaning job cuts.
Rather than hiding behind a gentle ___, the doctor said plainly and kindly what the scan showed.

misuse.text: He shouted a rude euphemism at the referee and was sent off.
misuse.why: A euphemism is a mild, polite replacement for a harsh word, not a rude insult.

misuse.text: The poem is full of euphemisms, such as comparing her eyes to stars.
misuse.why: Comparing things is a metaphor or simile; a euphemism softens something unpleasant or embarrassing.

phrases: ...is little more than a euphemism for...

synonyms.vs: Understatement makes something seem smaller than it is; a euphemism replaces an unpleasant term with a softer one.
Circumlocution is using many words to avoid saying something directly, not necessarily to soften it.
Doublespeak is deliberately misleading language, especially from governments or companies; a euphemism can simply be polite.

origin: From Greek euphemismos, from eu, 'well', and pheme, 'speaking': using words of good omen.

sense: a person's social and cultural surroundings
definition: The social and cultural surroundings in which someone lives or something happens.
nuance: Milieu is a formal word borrowed from French, used in history, sociology and literary criticism for the social world around a person, movement or work. It is neutral in tone. The plural is 'milieux' or 'milieus'.

examples.text: She grew up in a milieu of artists and musicians, so a creative career seemed perfectly normal to her.
Historians place the scientist's ideas firmly in the intellectual milieu of Victorian Britain.
The new director comes from a very different milieu, having spent her career in tech start-ups.
The report compares spending habits across households from several social milieux.
Honestly, a fancy dinner party isn't really my milieu; I'm happier at the pub.
The novel vividly captures the milieu of 1920s Paris, with its cafes, jazz clubs and exiled writers.

cloze.text: Raised on a quiet farm, he felt lost in the glamorous social ___ of London fashion, with its parties, rivalries and unwritten rules.
To understand the poet, read her work against the cultural ___ of post-war Liverpool: its clubs, music and politics.
The radicals of the 1840s shared the same social ___: the whole world of cafes, journals and friendships that surrounded them.

misuse.text: Draw a dot at the exact milieu of the circle.
misuse.why: Milieu means social surroundings; for the centre of a shape use 'middle' or 'centre', even though French milieu means middle.

misuse.text: He felt very milieu at the party, as if he didn't belong.
misuse.why: Milieu is a noun for social surroundings, not a feeling; say 'out of place', or 'it wasn't his milieu'.

phrases: ...must be read in the context of its social milieu.

synonyms.vs: Environment is broader and can be physical or natural; milieu is specifically social and cultural.
Setting is the time and place of a story or event; milieu is the social world of the people in it.
A circle is a group of people; a milieu is the whole social world around them.

origin: From French milieu, 'middle', made of mi, 'mid', and lieu, 'place'.

definition: Generally thought or claimed to be something, though this has not been proved.
nuance: Putative is formal and common in science, law and history. It labels something as assumed rather than confirmed, as in 'the putative father' or 'a putative cause'. It is more neutral than 'alleged', which suggests possible wrongdoing.

examples.text: The putative father of the child agreed to a DNA test to settle the question once and for all.
Researchers have identified a putative gene for the condition, but its role is not yet confirmed.
The putative author of the play may in fact have been a group of writers working together.
The putative benefits of the merger have yet to appear in the company's accounts.
So this is your putative masterpiece? It looks like a pile of socks.
The detective doubted the putative ransom note from the moment he saw the neat handwriting.

cloze.text: Investigators named a contaminated well as the ___ source of the outbreak, pending laboratory confirmation.
He was only the ___ owner of the painting: everyone assumed it was his, but no papers proved it.
Scientists described it as a ___ new species, assumed to be distinct but awaiting DNA tests to confirm it.

misuse.text: The putative results of the experiment proved the theory beyond any doubt.
misuse.why: Putative means assumed but unproven, so it clashes with proof beyond doubt.
