misuse.text: The court ordered the company to pay putative damages to punish its behaviour.
misuse.why: Putative means supposed; damages meant as punishment are 'punitive'.

synonyms.vs: Supposed is everyday and often sounds doubtful; putative is technical and more neutral.
Alleged is used mainly for claimed crimes or wrongdoing that have not been proved.
Presumed suggests a reasonable assumption that is probably true.

confusables.note: Punitive means intended as punishment.

origin: From Latin putativus, from putare, 'to think' or 'to reckon'.

sense: false or invalid, though seeming genuine
definition: Not genuine or valid, although it may appear to be at first.
nuance: Spurious is common in academic and legal writing for arguments, claims, links and documents that look valid but are not. In statistics, a 'spurious correlation' is a pattern in the data that does not come from one thing causing the other. It is clearly critical.

examples.text: He took the day off on the spurious grounds that his goldfish was feeling unwell.
Ice cream sales and sunburn both rise in summer, but the link between them is spurious: hot weather drives both.
The court dismissed the claim as spurious and ordered the company to pay costs.
Applicants who submit spurious documents will be disqualified immediately.
That's a spurious argument; you can't blame the rain for missing a week of lectures.
Scholars long ago exposed the letter as spurious, written decades after the king's death.

cloze.text: The two trends rose together only because a third factor drove both, so the correlation between them was ___.
Her excuse, that a seagull had stolen her homework, was obviously ___ and the teacher ignored it.
The scientist rejected the claim as ___: it looked convincing but rested on faulty data.

misuse.text: The spurious, carefully checked results were confirmed by three independent labs.
misuse.why: Spurious means false or invalid, so it contradicts results confirmed by independent checks.

misuse.text: He was spurious when he found that someone had scratched his car.
misuse.why: Spurious means false, not angry; the word wanted here is 'furious'.

phrases: This correlation may well be spurious, since...

synonyms.vs: Specious means plausible on the surface but wrong, usually of arguments; spurious also covers fake documents and data.
Bogus is informal and blunt.
False is general; spurious suggests something passing itself off as genuine.

origin: From Latin spurius, 'illegitimate', a word used of a child born outside marriage.

sense: explain an idea or theory in detail
definition: To explain or present an idea or theory carefully and in detail.
nuance: Expound is formal and often used about scholars, preachers and politicians setting out their views at length. It takes a direct object ('expound a theory') or 'on' ('expound on the dangers of'). It can hint that the speaker goes on rather long.

examples.text: In his first lecture, the professor expounded his theory step by step, explaining every part in careful detail.
The new party leader used her conference speech to expound her vision for the country.
Uncle Ray expounds on the history of every motorway to anyone who sits still long enough.
The guidance spends several pages expounding the principles behind the new funding rules.
The old sailor expounded on the dangers of the sea while we huddled by the fire.
Adam Smith expounds his theory of the division of labour in the opening chapters of The Wealth of Nations.

cloze.text: She spent the whole seminar ___ her theory, setting out each argument at length and in turn.
Asked a simple question, the minister began to ___ at great length on the history of taxation.
In the first chapter, the author ___ in detail the principles on which the rest of the book depends.

misuse.text: The balloon expounded with a loud bang when it touched the candle.
misuse.why: Expound means explain in detail; for bursting, the word is 'exploded'.

misuse.text: He expounded his answer in one quick word.
misuse.why: To expound is to explain at length, not to answer briefly.

synonyms.vs: Elaborate means add detail to something already said; expound means set out a whole idea systematically.
Explain is everyday; expound is formal and suggests length and authority.
Expatiate is rarer and suggests talking at tiresome length.

confusables.note: Propound means put forward an idea for others to consider.

origin: From Latin exponere, 'to put out' or 'to set forth'.

definition: Feeling or showing very strong and sincere passion for a belief, hope or cause.
nuance: Fervent describes intense, sincere feeling, often about beliefs, hopes and causes. It is common in 'a fervent supporter', 'a fervent believer' and 'a fervent hope'. It is usually neutral or approving, though it can hint at too much zeal.

examples.text: A fervent supporter of the local team, he has not missed a home match in thirty years.
It is my fervent hope that this agreement will bring a lasting peace.
The reformers' fervent belief in education led them to open schools in every parish.
She's a fervent believer in cold showers and tries to convert everyone she meets.
He wrote her fervent letters every day that summer, though she never answered one.
Fervent nationalism spread quickly through much of Europe in the decades before 1914.

cloze.text: Kneeling in the candlelit chapel, she whispered a ___ prayer, intense and heartfelt, for her son's safe return.
It is our ___ hope, held with all our hearts, that the missing hikers are found safe.
Even as a teenager she was a ___ admirer of Jane Austen, rereading the novels with almost religious devotion.

misuse.text: He gave the plan his fervent indifference, shrugging at every detail.
misuse.why: Fervent means intensely passionate, which contradicts indifference.

misuse.text: Don't touch the fervent oven door; it has only just been switched off.
misuse.why: Fervent now describes strong feelings, not physical heat; say 'the hot oven door'.

phrases: It is my fervent hope that...

synonyms.vs: Ardent is very close but slightly more literary, often used of admirers and lovers.
Zealous suggests eager action for a cause, sometimes taken too far.
Passionate is everyday and broader, covering love, anger and hobbies.

origin: From Latin fervere, 'to boil', so fervent feelings are boiling hot.

definition: Extremely peaceful, beautiful and happy, like a perfect scene from a story.
nuance: Idyllic describes places, times and lives that seem perfectly pleasant, often rural or simple. It is common in travel writing, property adverts and memories of childhood. In essays it can hint that the picture is too perfect to be true.

examples.text: They spent an idyllic week in a cottage by the lake, swimming every morning and reading all afternoon.
The island's idyllic beaches hide a serious problem with plastic washing in from the ocean.
Victorian painters often showed an idyllic countryside, ignoring the hardships of farm labour.
The brochure describes the hotel's setting as idyllic, surrounded by orchards and quiet lanes.
My childhood wasn't exactly idyllic, but we had a lot of fun.
Many memoirs paint an idyllic picture of village life that historians find hard to support.

cloze.text: The village seemed ___, not just pretty but peaceful and happy: thatched cottages, a duck pond and children playing on the green.
She had an ___ childhood: long summers by the sea, loving parents and not a care in the world.
The poem presents an ___ vision of country life, peaceful and lovely, free of hunger or hard work.

misuse.text: The idyllic hurricane tore the roofs off half the houses in town.
misuse.why: Idyllic means peaceful and beautiful, so it cannot describe a destructive storm.

misuse.text: He was idyllic about his chances, sure he would win without any training.
misuse.why: Idyllic describes peaceful, lovely scenes; for unrealistic hopes, use 'idealistic' or 'over-optimistic'.

phrases: Far from the idyllic image of..., ...

synonyms.vs: Picturesque means pretty to look at; idyllic adds peace and happiness.
Utopian describes an ideal society or plan, often unrealistic; idyllic describes a pleasant scene or time.
Blissful is about feeling extremely happy; idyllic is about a perfect setting or way of life.

confusables.note: Idealistic means believing in perfect ideals, often unrealistically.

origin: From idyll, a short poem about peaceful country life, from Greek eidyllion, 'little picture'.

definition: Brave and adventurous, willing to face danger or the unknown.
nuance: Intrepid is used for explorers, travellers, reporters and researchers who go into risky or unknown places. It is approving, and in modern speech it is often used humorously about small adventures. It suggests bold action rather than simply not feeling fear.

examples.text: The intrepid explorers crossed the frozen ice sheet on foot, facing storms and hunger for months.
An intrepid reporter spent a week aboard a fishing trawler in the North Sea in winter.
Victorian travellers such as Isabella Bird were intrepid, journeying alone across mountains and continents.
Our intrepid neighbour climbed onto the roof to rescue the cat.
The award recognises intrepid researchers whose fieldwork takes place in remote or dangerous regions.
Early polar expeditions relied on intrepid volunteers who knew they might never return.

cloze.text: Only the most ___ travellers attempt the route, which crosses deserts, rivers and wild mountains.
The ___ young pilot flew alone across the Atlantic, undaunted by storms, darkness and the unknown.
Fearless and adventurous, the ___ diver explored caves that no one had ever mapped.

misuse.text: The intrepid kitten hid under the bed whenever anyone spoke.
misuse.why: Intrepid means fearless, so it does not fit a kitten that hides in fear.

misuse.text: The soup was rather intrepid and needed more salt.
misuse.why: Intrepid means brave; for food with little flavour, the word is 'insipid'.

synonyms.vs: Fearless means feeling no fear; intrepid stresses bold action in dangerous or unknown situations.
Daring suggests taking risks for excitement, sometimes recklessly.
Dauntless is literary and stresses not being discouraged by difficulty.

confusables.note: Insipid means dull or lacking flavour.

origin: From Latin intrepidus, 'not alarmed', from in-, 'not', and trepidus, 'anxious'.

definition: Matching something in size, amount or seriousness; neither too much nor too little.
nuance: Proportionate is common in law, policy and ethics, especially for responses, punishments and costs. A 'proportionate response' fits the seriousness of what caused it. It is usually followed by 'to', as in 'proportionate to the risk'.

examples.text: The teacher believed punishments should be proportionate, so a forgotten pen earned only a gentle reminder.
Ministers insist that the new travel rules are a proportionate response to the risk.
In just war theory, force must be proportionate: the harm caused must not outweigh the good achieved.
Confiscating my phone for a whole term over one text? That's hardly proportionate.
Each member's contribution will be proportionate to their annual income.
The study found that funding for schools was not proportionate to pupil numbers in each region.

cloze.text: The fine should be ___ to the harm caused, not ten times larger.
Was the army's response ___, or did the force used far exceed the threat?
The penalty must be ___: severe enough to deter, but no harsher than the offence deserves.

misuse.text: A life sentence for parking on a yellow line would be perfectly proportionate.
misuse.why: Proportionate means fitting the seriousness of something, and a life sentence for a parking offence clearly does not.

misuse.text: The punishment was proportionate with the crime.
misuse.why: Proportionate is followed by 'to', not 'with': 'proportionate to the crime'.

phrases: ...must be proportionate to the risk posed by...
Whether such measures are proportionate depends on...

synonyms.vs: Proportional is common in maths and science for exact ratios; proportionate is preferred for fair responses and punishments.
Commensurate is more formal and usually describes pay or reward matching skill, effort or experience.
Appropriate means suitable in general; proportionate is specifically about the right size or degree.

origin: From Latin pro portione, 'according to its share'.

definition: Badly made or done, through carelessness or the use of cheap materials.
nuance: Shoddy is a critical word for poor workmanship, goods, research or service. It is slightly informal but common in news and reviews. 'Shoddy treatment' extends it to behaving badly towards people.

examples.text: Those shoddy shelves collapsed within a week because the builder used cheap wood and too few screws.
An inquiry blamed shoddy construction for the collapse of the footbridge.
Reviewers rejected the paper, criticising its shoddy methods and tiny sample.
Customers who receive shoddy goods are entitled to a refund or a replacement.
She was tired of the shoddy way he treated her friends, always late and never sorry.
Shoddy referencing can cost marks even when the argument itself is strong.

cloze.text: The house was full of ___ repairs: taped-up pipes, crooked tiles and doors that would not shut.
Cheap, ___ goods that fall apart after one use are bad for both customers and the planet.
The builders' ___ workmanship, rushed and careless, meant the roof leaked within a month.

misuse.text: The carpenter's shoddy workmanship won him first prize at the furniture show.
misuse.why: Shoddy means badly made, so it would not win a prize for craftsmanship.

misuse.text: We sat in a shoddy corner of the garden, out of the hot sun.
misuse.why: Shoddy means poorly made or done; for a place out of the sun, the word is 'shady'.

synonyms.vs: Substandard is formal and means below a required level; shoddy adds a sense of carelessness.
Flimsy means weak and easily broken; shoddy covers any poor workmanship.
Slapdash describes careless, hurried work rather than cheap materials.

confusables.note: Shady means sheltered from the sun, or informally, dishonest.

origin: Shoddy was first the name of cheap cloth made from recycled wool, which wore out quickly; the word then came to mean poor quality in general.

definition: Very determined to keep going or hold on, and refusing to give up easily.
nuance: Tenacious is usually approving, describing people who persist despite difficulty. It also describes things that hold firmly, such as a 'tenacious grip', or beliefs and myths that are hard to shift. Do not confuse it with tenuous, which means weak.

examples.text: The tenacious reporter phoned the minister's office every day for a year until she finally got an interview.
My little brother is tenacious; he'll ask for a dog every single day until Mum gives in.
Some myths of popular science, such as the idea that we use only ten per cent of our brains, are remarkably tenacious.
The ivy kept a tenacious grip on the old wall, impossible to pull away.
The committee praised her tenacious efforts to secure funding for the new clinic.
Darwin was a tenacious observer who spent eight years studying barnacles.

cloze.text: Despite dozens of rejections, the ___ author kept sending out her manuscript until a publisher said yes.
The little terrier was ___: once it had the rope in its teeth, nothing could make it let go.
Old beliefs can be ___: they cling on long after the evidence against them has piled up.

misuse.text: She was so tenacious that she gave up after her first attempt.
misuse.why: Tenacious means refusing to give up, so it contradicts quitting after one try.

misuse.text: The link between the two events is tenacious at best.
misuse.why: For a weak or slight link, the word is 'tenuous'; tenacious means holding on firmly.

phrases: ...proved remarkably tenacious in the face of...

synonyms.vs: Persistent means continuing over time; tenacious adds firm determination and grip.
Dogged suggests stubborn, plodding effort, sometimes without much flair.
Resolute stresses firm purpose and courage in a decision, rather than holding on over time.

confusables.note: Tenuous means very weak or slight.

origin: From Latin tenax, 'holding fast', from tenere, 'to hold'.

sense: the growth of towns and cities
definition: The process by which towns and cities grow and more of a population comes to live in them.
nuance: Urbanisation is a key term in geography, history, economics and development studies. It describes a long-term process rather than a single city, and is often linked to industrialisation and migration. British English usually spells it with an s.

examples.text: As factories opened, rapid urbanisation drew millions of families from the farms into crowded cities.
Rapid urbanisation in West Africa is putting pressure on housing and transport.
The module examines the links between urbanisation, disease and public health in Victorian Britain.
The report recommends that planners prepare for continued urbanisation by investing in parks and green spaces.
Our village used to have fields all round it; urbanisation has basically swallowed it up.
From the hilltop she could see the creeping urbanisation that had replaced her grandfather's orchards.

cloze.text: The rapid growth of cities, known as ___, transformed Britain during the Industrial Revolution.
As ___ continues, the share of the world's people living in towns and cities keeps rising year after year.
Geographers link ___ to industrial growth, as workers leave the countryside for jobs in towns.

misuse.text: The urbanisation of the old farmhouse made it feel modern and stylish.
misuse.why: Urbanisation describes cities growing and people moving into them, not modernising a single building.

misuse.text: The region is seeing rapid urbanisation as thousands of families leave the cities for quiet villages.
misuse.why: Moving from cities to the countryside is the opposite of urbanisation; it is called counter-urbanisation.

synonyms.vs: Industrialisation is the growth of factories and industry; urbanisation is the growth of cities, which often follows it.
Suburbanisation is the spread of housing around a city's edges rather than the growth of cities in general.
Development is much broader, covering economic and social change of all kinds.

confusables.note: Urbane means polite, confident and sophisticated.

definition: A feeling or state of deep, lasting hostility between people or groups.
nuance: Enmity is a formal, rather literary word for long-standing hostility, often between nations, families or rivals. It is stronger and more lasting than dislike. It usually appears as 'enmity between' or 'enmity towards'.

examples.text: The enmity between the two families began with a quarrel over a field and lasted for three generations.
Historians trace the enmity between the two empires back to a disputed border.
Despite years of public enmity, the rival leaders shook hands warmly at the summit.
There's real enmity between those two flatmates; they haven't spoken since the fridge incident.
The treaty aimed to replace centuries of enmity with trade and cooperation.
Old enmities resurfaced when the two clubs were drawn against each other in the cup.

cloze.text: Decades of bitter ___ between the neighbouring states finally ended with a peace treaty.
Instead of friendship, the long feud left only ___, a cold and lasting hatred on both sides.
Once close friends, the two poets ended their lives in bitter ___, each treating the other as a sworn foe.

misuse.text: Their deep enmity made them the closest of friends.
misuse.why: Enmity means hostility, so it cannot produce close friendship.

misuse.text: He felt a brief enmity when the bus was late, but forgot about it at once.
misuse.why: Enmity is deep, lasting hostility, usually between people, not a moment of annoyance.

synonyms.vs: Hostility can be open and short-term; enmity suggests deep, long-lasting ill will.
Animosity is strong dislike that shows itself; enmity is more formal and often mutual.
Antagonism stresses active opposition, as in a rivalry or conflict.

confusables.note: Amity means friendship, the opposite of enmity.

origin: From Old French enemistie, from Latin inimicus, 'enemy', literally 'not a friend'.

definition: To become less strong or intense, or to make something do so.
nuance: Abate is formal and used mostly about storms, floods, pain, anger and crises dying down. It is often used without an object ('the storm abated'), and 'show no sign of abating' is a common phrase. In law it can also mean reduce or end a nuisance.

examples.text: We waited in the cafe until the storm abated, then walked home under clear skies.
The flooding shows no sign of abating, and more rain is forecast for the weekend.
Her anger abates as quickly as it flares, so wait ten minutes before you talk to her.
Researchers measured how quickly the children's anxiety abated after their first week at a new school.
Symptoms usually abate within a week, although tiredness may last longer.
New regulations are intended to abate pollution from older diesel engines.

cloze.text: We waited in the harbour until the gale had ___, its winds weakening enough for the ferry to sail safely.
The pain should ___ within a few hours, but call the doctor if it gets worse.
Despite the minister's apology, public anger showed no sign of ___.

misuse.text: The storm abated, and the winds grew stronger all night.
misuse.why: Abate means become weaker, so it contradicts winds growing stronger.

misuse.text: The teacher abated the noisy students until they were quiet.
misuse.why: You can abate a problem such as noise or pollution, but not people.

synonyms.vs: Subside also means calm down, and can describe water levels falling or ground sinking.
Diminish means become smaller in size or amount in general; abate suits forces and feelings.
Wane suggests slow, gradual decline, like the moon or interest over time.
Ease is everyday and gentle; abate is formal.

confusables.note: Abet means help someone do wrong, as in 'aid and abet'.

origin: From Old French abatre, 'to beat down' or 'to knock down'.

definition: The crime of encouraging people, through speech or writing, to rebel against the government.
nuance: Sedition is a legal and historical term for stirring up rebellion rather than taking part in it. It appears in history, law and politics, often in debates about free speech. Unlike treason, it usually involves words rather than acts.

examples.text: The poet was charged with sedition for printing pamphlets that urged the people to overthrow the king.
In the 1790s, several British radicals who called for political reform were tried for sedition.
The journalist was cleared of sedition, and the judge stressed the importance of a free press.
Several countries have abolished their old sedition laws, arguing that they threatened free speech.
Relax, suggesting a longer lunch break isn't exactly sedition.
Historians still debate whether the speech was genuine sedition or simply harsh criticism of the government.

cloze.text: He was not accused of treason but of ___: stirring up rebellion through his speeches and pamphlets.
Under the old ___ laws, printing words that encouraged revolt against the king could lead to prison.
The editor was arrested for ___, accused of urging readers in print to rise up against the government.

misuse.text: The soldiers were praised for their sedition, staying loyal to the king throughout the war.
misuse.why: Sedition means stirring up rebellion, the opposite of loyalty.

misuse.text: He committed sedition by stealing a bicycle from outside the library.
misuse.why: Sedition is encouraging rebellion against the state, not an ordinary crime such as theft.

phrases: The line between legitimate criticism and sedition...

synonyms.vs: Treason is betraying your country, for example by helping an enemy; sedition is encouraging rebellion, usually through words.
Rebellion is the uprising itself; sedition is stirring people up towards one.
Incitement is encouraging any crime or violence; sedition is aimed specifically at the state.

confusables.note: Sedation means calming someone with drugs.

origin: From Latin seditio, literally 'a going apart', from sed-, 'apart', and ire, 'to go'.

sense: the art of powerful public speaking
definition: The skill or art of giving formal speeches that move and persuade an audience.
nuance: Oratory is used for powerful public speaking, especially by politicians, lawyers and preachers. It is usually admiring, but 'empty oratory' suggests fine words without substance. Do not confuse it with an oratory, a small chapel for prayer.

examples.text: The crowd rose to its feet, moved by the young candidate's passionate oratory about rebuilding the town.
Classical schools trained students in oratory, teaching them to structure an argument and hold an audience.
Churchill's wartime oratory is still studied for its rhythm and its simple, vivid language.
Who knew Dad was capable of such oratory? He had the whole wedding laughing and crying.
Members are reminded that proposals will be judged on their evidence, not on the oratory used to present them.
The old preacher's oratory filled the chapel, rising and falling like the sea outside.

cloze.text: Even her opponents admired her gift for ___: when she rose to speak, a packed hall fell silent for an hour.
Debating clubs help students develop their ___, the art of making powerful public speeches.
Great ___ depends on delivery as much as on words: the pauses, the rise and fall of the voice, the eye contact with the crowd.

misuse.text: She wrote the essay in beautiful oratory, full of long and elegant sentences.
misuse.why: Oratory is spoken aloud to an audience; for fine writing use 'prose' or 'style'.

misuse.text: He gave an oratory to the class about his summer holiday.
misuse.why: Oratory is a skill or style of speaking, not a single speech; say 'gave a speech'.

phrases: ...relied more on oratory than on evidence.

synonyms.vs: Rhetoric is the art of persuasion in speech or writing and is often used critically; oratory is specifically about speaking aloud.
Eloquence is fluent, expressive language in any form; oratory is the public performance of it.

confusables.note: An oratorio is a long piece of religious music for choir and orchestra.

origin: From Latin orator, 'speaker', from orare, 'to speak or pray', which is why an oratory is also a small chapel.

sense: a long angry speech of criticism
definition: A long, angry speech or piece of writing that attacks or criticises someone.
nuance: A tirade is angry, one-sided and usually long: the speaker attacks rather than discusses. It is critical in tone and used of outbursts in politics, sport and online. It is often followed by 'against' or 'about'.

examples.text: After losing the match, the coach launched into a ten-minute tirade against the referee, shouting and waving his arms.
The novel opens with a father's furious tirade about his son's wasted education.
Historians note that the pamphlet was less a reasoned argument than a tirade against the new tax.
I only asked if she'd seen my charger, and I got a tirade about my messy room.
His online tirades against critics eventually cost him two sponsorship deals.
The chair asked members to raise concerns calmly, as personal tirades would not be recorded in the minutes.

cloze.text: Furious about the delay, the passenger launched into a long ___ against the airline, shouting at staff for ten minutes without a pause.
Instead of answering the question calmly, the minister delivered a furious ___ against his critics, attacking the press and the opposition in turn.
The manager was fined after his post-match ___ against referees: long, angry attacks in which he accused them of bias.

misuse.text: The speaker gave a gentle tirade, praising everyone who had helped with the event.
misuse.why: A tirade is angry and critical, so it cannot be gentle or full of praise.

misuse.text: The tirade between the two neighbours went on for weeks, with letters going back and forth.
misuse.why: A tirade is one person's angry speech, not an exchange; for a long quarrel use 'feud' or 'dispute'.

phrases: What began as criticism became a tirade.

synonyms.vs: Rant is informal and can be comic; tirade is more formal and stresses anger and attack.
A diatribe is a bitter attack, often written and more sustained; a tirade is usually spoken and heated.
A harangue is a long, forceful lecture aimed at an audience; tirade stresses anger rather than persuasion.

origin: From French tirade, 'a long speech', from Italian tirata, 'a volley', from tirare, 'to pull or fire'.

sense: a clash between things that do not fit
definition: A clash or lack of harmony between sounds, ideas, beliefs or actions that do not fit together.
nuance: Dissonance began as a music term for notes that clash, and is now common in academic writing about ideas and behaviour. 'Cognitive dissonance' is the discomfort of holding beliefs that contradict each other or your actions. It is formal and usually neutral or critical.

examples.text: There is a strange dissonance between the company's green adverts and its rising pollution figures.
Cognitive dissonance theory suggests that people change their beliefs to match what they have already done.
The composer uses dissonance in the final bars, so the piece ends on an uneasy, unresolved chord.
The dissonance between his cheerful voice and his tired eyes told her something was wrong.
I get this weird dissonance, buying cheap clothes while telling everyone I care about waste.
The review identified several dissonances between the policy as written and actual practice on the wards.

cloze.text: Smokers who know the health risks often feel cognitive ___, the discomfort of acting against their own beliefs.
Instead of harmony and consonance, the composer chose ___: harsh, clashing chords that leave listeners uneasy.
Like two notes that refuse to blend, the charity's message of simple living and its lavish headquarters created a jarring ___.

misuse.text: The choir sang in perfect dissonance, every voice blending beautifully.
misuse.why: Dissonance means a clash of sounds; voices blending beautifully are in harmony.

misuse.text: There was a dissonance of about five miles between the two villages.
misuse.why: Dissonance is a clash between sounds or ideas, not a physical gap; use 'distance'.

phrases: There is a striking dissonance between... and...

synonyms.vs: Discord is often about conflict between people; dissonance more often describes a clash between ideas, sounds or actions.
Inconsistency is neutral and logical; dissonance adds a sense of tension or discomfort.
Incongruity stresses that something looks oddly out of place; dissonance stresses an uncomfortable clash.

confusables.note: Dissidence means open disagreement with a government or official policy.

origin: From Latin dissonare, 'to sound different', from dis-, 'apart', and sonare, 'to sound'.

definition: To criticise or tell someone off severely for something they have done wrong.
nuance: Chastise is a formal word for sharp criticism, often from someone with authority: a teacher, a judge, a newspaper. It usually takes 'for': 'chastised for being late'. The older sense, to punish physically, is now rare.

examples.text: Their mother chastised them for tracking mud across the freshly cleaned kitchen floor.
The report chastises the department for ignoring repeated safety warnings.
Medieval sermons often chastised listeners for vanity, greed and idleness.
Don't chastise yourself over one bad exam; everyone has an off day.
The regulator publicly chastised the bank but stopped short of issuing a fine.
Rather than chastising pupils for mistakes, the study recommends treating errors as part of learning.

cloze.text: In a sharp public statement, the regulator ___ the bank for its failures, scolding it severely but stopping short of a fine.
My grandmother still ___ me for wearing shoes indoors, scolding me as if I were six.
The strict abbess was forever ___ the young nuns for small faults, scolding them sharply in front of the whole convent.

misuse.text: The teacher chastised the class for their excellent results.
misuse.why: To chastise is to criticise someone for doing wrong, not for doing well.

misuse.text: The new law chastises tax evasion with heavy fines.
misuse.why: You chastise a person, not a crime; for laws dealing with crimes use 'punishes' or 'penalises'.

synonyms.vs: Scold is everyday and often about children; chastise is more formal and can be public.
Castigate is stronger and more formal, suggesting harsh, often public criticism.
A reprimand is often official, from an employer or authority; chastise is more general.
Rebuke suggests a sharp, short telling-off; chastise can be longer and harsher.

confusables.note: Chasten means to make someone humbler, often through a bad experience: a chastening defeat.

origin: Related to chasten and castigate, which come from Latin castigare, 'to correct or punish'.

sense: being sacred or too important to violate
definition: The quality of being holy, or so important that it must be respected and protected.
nuance: Sanctity is used in religious contexts and, more often in essays, for things treated as almost sacred: 'the sanctity of life', 'the sanctity of the home'. Writers use it when something is precious and must not be broken or interfered with. It is formal and serious.

examples.text: Visitors spoke only in whispers inside the temple, aware of the sanctity of the place.
Medical ethics has long debated how the sanctity of life should be weighed against a patient's own wishes.
In our house nobody checks their phone at Sunday lunch; Mum protects its sanctity fiercely.
The ruling reaffirmed the sanctity of the ballot, stressing that every vote must remain secret.
Courts have long upheld the sanctity of contracts: agreements freely made must be honoured.
Anthropologists describe how the sanctity of certain groves protected them from logging for centuries.

cloze.text: Doctors and philosophers still debate the ___ of human life: whether it is so precious that it must never be deliberately ended.
Pilgrims removed their shoes to respect the ___ of the shrine, a place they considered holy.
The judge spoke of the ___ of contracts, insisting that a promise freely made must be kept.

misuse.text: After weeks of stress, a quiet holiday helped her recover her sanctity.
misuse.why: Sanctity means holiness or sacredness; the word for a sound, healthy mind is 'sanity'.

misuse.text: He was praised for his sanctity in finishing the project on time.
misuse.why: Sanctity is about being sacred, not about efficiency or reliability; use 'diligence'.

phrases: The principle of the sanctity of life holds that...

synonyms.vs: Holiness is strictly religious; sanctity can also describe non-religious things treated as untouchable.
Inviolability is legal and technical, stressing that something must not be broken; sanctity adds a sense of reverence.
Sacredness is plainer and broader; sanctity sounds more formal and often appears in fixed phrases.

confusables.note: Sanity means having a healthy, sound mind.
Sanctimony means acting as if you are morally better than others.

origin: From Latin sanctitas, 'holiness', from sanctus, 'holy', the source of saint and sanctuary.

definition: To read or examine something carefully and in detail.
nuance: Peruse traditionally means to read with care, and that is the safe sense in formal writing. Many people now use it to mean 'skim' or 'glance through', so the word is easily misunderstood. If you mean a quick look, write skim instead.

examples.text: Before signing, she perused the contract line by line, checking every clause twice.
The historian spent months perusing parish records for any mention of the family.
Each reviewer peruses the manuscript closely before making a recommendation to the editor.
He perused the letter slowly, rereading the last paragraph three times.
Investigators have perused thousands of emails in search of evidence of price fixing.
I'll peruse your essay properly tonight and send you detailed notes in the morning.

cloze.text: Good lawyers do not just read a contract; they ___ it, studying every clause slowly and closely for hidden risks.
She spent the afternoon ___ the old diary, reading each entry with care and noting every date it mentioned.
The examiner ___ the thesis page by page, a slow and careful read that filled the margins with comments.

misuse.text: I perused the article in about ten seconds and then closed it.
misuse.why: In careful writing peruse means read thoroughly, so ten seconds is far too quick; say 'skimmed' or 'glanced at'.

misuse.text: She perused down the high street, looking in shop windows.
misuse.why: Peruse means read or examine something, not walk; for a slow walk use 'strolled' or 'wandered'.

synonyms.vs: Scrutinise is stronger, suggesting a critical search for faults; peruse is simply careful reading.
Study is everyday and broader; peruse is formal and mostly used for texts.
Examine can be used for anything, not just texts; peruse is mainly about reading.

confusables.note: Pursue means to chase or follow; it has similar letters but a different meaning.

sense: a person indifferent or hostile to culture
definition: A person who does not value art, literature or learning, and may look down on them.
nuance: Calling someone a philistine is an insult, suggesting they are narrow and dismissive of culture. It is often used jokingly about yourself: 'I'm a philistine about opera'. It can also be an adjective, as in 'philistine attitudes'.

examples.text: Only a philistine, the old painter muttered, would hang a masterpiece above the radiator.
I'm a total philistine when it comes to ballet; I fell asleep in the second act.
Nineteenth-century critics attacked the middle-class philistines who valued profit above beauty.
The council was accused of acting like philistines when it cut the arts budget to zero.
The governors rejected the charge that closing the music department made them philistines.
In Culture and Anarchy, Matthew Arnold mocks the philistine who judges everything by its practical use.

cloze.text: He calls opera a waste of money and novels a waste of time, so his friends call him a ___.
Critics said only ___, people with no time for books or learning, would close a library to build a car park.
Don't be such a ___ about art: the gallery is free, and you might actually enjoy the paintings.

misuse.text: She is a real philistine, spending every weekend in museums and concert halls.
misuse.why: A philistine has no interest in culture, so a keen museum-goer is the opposite.

misuse.text: He was a great philistine of the arts, giving millions to theatres and galleries.
misuse.why: That describes a patron or philanthropist; a philistine is indifferent or hostile to culture.

synonyms.vs: Lowbrow describes unsophisticated tastes or things; philistine suggests active hostility or indifference to culture.
Barbarian is stronger and broader, suggesting crude or uncivilised behaviour, not just a lack of interest in the arts.

confusables.note: A philanthropist gives money to good causes, including the arts.

origin: From the biblical Philistines, enemies of the Israelites. German students used Philister for townspeople outside the university, and Matthew Arnold popularised the English sense in the 1860s.

sense: extremely complicated and hard to follow
definition: So complicated and twisting that it is hard to follow or understand.
nuance: Convoluted is a critical word for arguments, sentences, plots and systems that are more complicated than they need to be. It is common in reviews and essay feedback. Complex can be neutral; convoluted implies the complication is a fault.

examples.text: The instructions were so convoluted that we gave up and built the shelf without them.
The essay's argument is convoluted, with each paragraph adding a new exception to the last.
Critics loved the acting but found the plot convoluted and hard to follow.
The audit found that convoluted approval procedures were delaying urgent repairs.
She gave a convoluted excuse involving a lost dog, a flat tyre and her cousin's wedding.
Legal scholars have criticised the convoluted wording of the statute, which allows several readings.

cloze.text: His explanation was not just complicated but ___, twisting back on itself so often that nobody could follow it.
Rewrite this tangled, ___ sentence: its five clauses wind around each other and the reader loses track halfway.
The film's plot is needlessly ___, winding through three timelines and two narrators before a final twist that makes no sense.

misuse.text: The instructions were so convoluted that a small child could follow them easily.
misuse.why: Convoluted means hard to follow; instructions a child can follow are simple or clear.

misuse.text: Her face looked convoluted with anger as she shouted at him.
misuse.why: Convoluted describes arguments, plans or shapes, not faces; for a face twisted by anger use 'contorted'.

phrases: The argument becomes increasingly convoluted when...

synonyms.vs: Complex is neutral and can even be praise; convoluted suggests needless, confusing complication.
Intricate is usually admiring, suggesting fine detail; convoluted is critical.
Tortuous suggests a long, twisting path or slow process; convoluted stresses tangled reasoning or wording.

confusables.note: Contorted means twisted out of its normal shape, often of a face or body.

origin: From Latin convolutus, 'rolled together', from volvere, 'to roll'.

sense: in bad condition from age or neglect
definition: Old, broken and in very poor condition because nobody has looked after it.
nuance: Dilapidated is used about buildings, vehicles and furniture that have been allowed to fall apart. It suggests long neglect rather than sudden damage. It is common in news reports about housing, schools and towns.

examples.text: The dilapidated farmhouse had broken windows, a sagging roof and weeds growing through the floor.
Inspectors found that dozens of schools were teaching pupils in dilapidated classrooms.
We drove a dilapidated old van across Europe, and somehow it only broke down once.
The study links dilapidated housing to higher rates of asthma among children.
Funding is sought to restore the dilapidated pier, which has been closed to the public since 2015.
Urban historians trace how dilapidated warehouses became fashionable flats in the 1990s.

cloze.text: The old cinema is still open, but decades without repairs have left it ___: the roof leaks and the seats are torn.
The family still lived in the ___ cottage, though its roof sagged and its walls had crumbled after years of neglect.
Tenants complained about living in neglected, ___ flats with broken lifts, damp walls and rotten windows.

misuse.text: The brand-new hotel looked dilapidated, with gleaming floors and fresh paint.
misuse.why: Dilapidated means falling apart from neglect, not new and well kept.

misuse.text: After the marathon I felt completely dilapidated and went straight to bed.
misuse.why: Dilapidated describes buildings and objects, not people; for tiredness use 'exhausted' or 'drained'.

phrases: ...had been left in a dilapidated state.
Many of the buildings were dilapidated, with...

synonyms.vs: Run-down is everyday and can describe whole areas; dilapidated is more formal and mostly for buildings and objects.
Derelict means abandoned as well as decaying; a dilapidated house may still be lived in.
Ramshackle suggests something badly built and likely to collapse; dilapidated stresses decay over time.

origin: From Latin dilapidare, 'to squander', literally 'to scatter like stones', from lapis, 'stone'.

definition: A very strong, passionate feeling or enthusiasm for something.
nuance: Fervour describes intense, often shared feeling about a cause, belief or event: religious, patriotic or revolutionary fervour. It can be admiring, but it can also hint that the feeling is excessive or uncritical. British English spells it fervour; American English fervor.

examples.text: Fans sang with such fervour that the whole stadium seemed to shake.
Historians have traced how revolutionary fervour spread through Paris in the summer of 1789.
He spoke of the sea with a quiet fervour, as if describing an old friend.
My brother talks about his football team with almost religious fervour.
The report warns that the fervour surrounding new technologies can lead investors to ignore risks.
The essay examines how the religious fervour of the Reformation reshaped everyday life.

cloze.text: Students marched through the capital in a wave of revolutionary ___, burning with passion for change.
Her early ___ for the project, a burning, almost feverish passion, faded once the long, dull paperwork began.
The new leader was greeted with almost religious ___, as followers wept and chanted her name.

misuse.text: He listened to the dull lecture with complete fervour, half asleep in his seat.
misuse.why: Fervour is intense passion, which clashes with boredom and sleepiness.

misuse.text: The patient's fervour rose to 39 degrees overnight.
misuse.why: Fervour means passionate feeling, not body temperature; the word you want is 'fever'.

phrases: The initial fervour soon gave way to...

synonyms.vs: Zeal is energetic devotion that drives action; fervour is more about the intensity of feeling.
Enthusiasm is everyday and milder; fervour is stronger and often shared by a crowd.
Ardour is literary and often romantic; fervour more often describes beliefs and causes.

confusables.note: A fever is a high body temperature.

origin: From Latin fervor, 'heat', from fervere, 'to boil'.

sense: too small in amount or quality
definition: Too small in amount, size or quality to be enough.
nuance: Meagre is used for amounts that are disappointingly small: wages, savings, rations, evidence, results. It is critical, suggesting something falls short of what is needed. British English spells it meagre; American English meager.

examples.text: Many care workers say their meagre wages barely cover rent and food.
The evidence for the claim is meagre: two small studies, neither of them repeated.
Breakfast was a meagre slice of dry toast and half a cup of cold tea.
Is that all we get? That's a pretty meagre portion for twelve pounds.
Despite meagre resources, the charity supported over a thousand families last year.
Medieval peasants struggled to survive on meagre harvests in years of poor weather.

cloze.text: The refugees survived on ___ rations: a little rice and a cup of water each day.
Three years of digging produced only ___ results: a few broken pots, far too little to justify the cost.
Pensioners struggled to heat their homes on such ___ incomes, barely enough to cover the basics.

misuse.text: They enjoyed a meagre feast, with ten courses and endless wine.
misuse.why: Meagre means too small or too little, so it cannot describe a huge feast.

misuse.text: He is very meagre with his money and never buys anyone a drink.
misuse.why: Meagre describes amounts, not people; for someone unwilling to spend use 'mean' or 'stingy'.

phrases: The evidence for this is meagre.

synonyms.vs: Paltry is more scornful, suggesting an amount is insultingly small.
Scanty often describes supplies or clothing; meagre is common for money, food and evidence.
Sparse means thinly spread out; meagre means too little in total.

origin: From Old French maigre, 'thin', from Latin macer, 'lean'.

sense: narrow in outlook, only locally minded
definition: Only interested in local matters and narrow in outlook, ignoring the wider world.
nuance: Parochial is a critical word for attitudes, debates or concerns that are small-minded or inward-looking. It comes from 'parish' and still has a neutral church sense, as in 'parochial records'. In essays it usually criticises a narrow focus.

examples.text: While the region faced flooding, the councillors spent an hour arguing about one parking space, a strangely parochial debate.
Historians have criticised earlier studies of the war as parochial, since they relied only on British sources.
Moving abroad made me realise how parochial my view of the world had been.
The review warned that a parochial approach to hiring, drawing almost entirely on the university's own graduates, limited fresh ideas.
To the villagers, London was a distant rumour; their world was small and cheerfully parochial.
Comparative literature challenges parochial reading habits by setting texts from different cultures side by side.

cloze.text: Her travels made her impatient with the ___ gossip of her home town, which ignored the wider world.
The newspaper was criticised for its ___ outlook: it covered village fairs but never international news.
The council's view was narrowly ___: it never looked beyond the boundaries of its own parish.

misuse.text: Her parochial interests ranged across every continent and culture.
misuse.why: Parochial means narrow and local, so it clashes with interests that span the world.

misuse.text: He is very parochial and goes to church every single Sunday.
misuse.why: Used of people, parochial means narrow-minded, not religious; for a regular churchgoer use 'devout'.

phrases: Far from being parochial, the study...

synonyms.vs: Insular suggests being cut off and uninterested in outsiders, often of a group or country; parochial stresses local focus.
Provincial suggests unsophisticated tastes away from the capital; parochial means narrow in what you care about.
Narrow-minded is everyday and about intolerance; parochial is formal and about limited scope.

origin: From Late Latin parochia, 'parish': a parochial view is one that does not look beyond the parish boundary.

definition: Confused and unable to understand something, especially something unexpected or hard to explain.
nuance: Perplexed describes puzzlement, often with a hint of worry, at something that does not make sense. It is slightly formal but common in news and fiction. It describes people and their expressions, not the problem itself; the problem is perplexing.

examples.text: She looked perplexed when the machine took her money but gave her no ticket.
Scientists were perplexed by the bees' sudden disappearance from the valley.
Early astronomers were perplexed by the way some planets seemed to move backwards across the sky.
I'm honestly perplexed: why would anyone queue for six hours for a sandwich?
Members of the panel were perplexed that the figures in the two reports did not match.
Readers are often perplexed by the poem's final line, which seems to contradict everything before it.

cloze.text: The students looked ___ as the professor wrote a formula none of them had seen, frowning and scratching their heads.
Doctors were ___ by her symptoms, which matched no illness they had ever seen.
Astronomers were deeply ___ by the signal, unable to explain where it came from or why it repeated every eighteen minutes.

misuse.text: The instructions were perplexed, so nobody could build the table.
misuse.why: People are perplexed; instructions that confuse people are 'perplexing' or 'confusing'.

misuse.text: She felt perplexed and happy because everything finally made sense.
misuse.why: Perplexed means confused, so it clashes with everything making sense.

synonyms.vs: Puzzled is everyday and mild; perplexed is a little more formal and can suggest worry.
Baffled is stronger, meaning completely unable to understand.
Bewildered suggests being overwhelmed and disoriented, often by too much happening at once.

origin: From Latin perplexus, 'tangled or confused', from per-, 'thoroughly', and plexus, 'woven'.

sense: serious and gloomy, or dark in colour
definition: Serious, sad and gloomy in mood, or dark and dull in colour.
nuance: Sombre describes moods, occasions, music and colours that are dark and serious, often in a respectful way, as at a funeral or memorial. It is neutral rather than critical. British English spells it sombre; American English somber.

examples.text: The mood at the memorial service was sombre, and few people spoke above a whisper.
She chose a sombre navy dress for her grandfather's funeral.
Why is everyone looking so sombre? We won the match!
The painter's late works shift to a sombre palette of browns and deep greens.
The chair opened the meeting on a sombre note, paying tribute to a colleague who had died.
Historians read the sombre tone of the king's final letters as evidence of his failing health.

cloze.text: The funeral was a ___ occasion: everyone dressed in black and spoke in low voices.
After the bad news, the mood in the usually cheerful dressing room turned dark and ___: heads bowed, and nobody spoke.
The film's ___ colours, mostly greys and dark blues, match its sad and serious story.

misuse.text: The party was wonderfully sombre, with loud music and dancing until dawn.
misuse.why: Sombre means serious and gloomy, the opposite of a lively party.

misuse.text: He stayed sombre all night because he was driving and drank only water.
misuse.why: Sombre means grave or gloomy; for someone who has not drunk alcohol use 'sober'.

phrases: The poem ends on a sombre note...

synonyms.vs: Gloomy is everyday and can be critical; sombre is more dignified and often respectful.
Solemn stresses formality and seriousness, as at a ceremony; sombre adds sadness or darkness.
Grave suggests serious concern about something important; sombre is more about mood and atmosphere.

confusables.note: Sober means not drunk, or calm and serious; it overlaps with sombre for colours and moods.

definition: Without a clear shape, structure or form, and so vague and hard to define.
nuance: Amorphous is used for shapes, groups and ideas that lack clear edges or organisation. In essays it is often mildly critical, describing a concept or movement too vague to pin down. In science it describes solids, such as glass, that have no crystal structure.

examples.text: Through the fog, the ship was just an amorphous grey shape with no clear outline.
Critics argue that 'wellbeing' is an amorphous concept that is difficult to measure.
The protest movement remained amorphous, with no leaders, no list of demands and no name.
Glass is an amorphous solid: its atoms lack the regular pattern found in crystals.
My plans for the summer are still pretty amorphous, to be honest.
The committee found the proposal too amorphous to fund and asked for clear aims and deadlines.

cloze.text: Through the frosted glass she could see only an ___ mass of colour, without any definite shape, form or edges.
Without a leader or any structure, the group stayed ___ and slowly fell apart.
His job title is vague and ___: nobody, including him, can say where his role begins or ends.

misuse.text: The amorphous crystal had perfectly regular, sharp edges.
misuse.why: Amorphous means without a definite shape or structure, so sharp regular edges are the opposite.

misuse.text: She felt amorphous towards him, neither loving nor hating him.
misuse.why: Amorphous describes shapes, groups or ideas, not feelings; for mixed feelings use 'ambivalent'.

phrases: The term is too amorphous to...

synonyms.vs: Shapeless is plain and mostly physical; amorphous also applies to ideas, groups and organisations.
Nebulous means hazy and unclear, mostly of ideas; amorphous stresses a lack of structure or form.
Vague is everyday and about unclear meaning; amorphous suggests no defined boundaries or structure at all.

confusables.note: Amorous means showing romantic or sexual desire.

origin: From Greek amorphos, 'shapeless', from a-, 'without', and morphe, 'form'.

sense: lack of balance or equality between sides
definition: A lack of balance or equality between two sides, parts or groups.
nuance: Asymmetry describes shapes whose two halves differ, but in essays it often means an imbalance of power, information or treatment between groups. 'Information asymmetry' and 'power asymmetry' are common in economics and politics. It is neutral and analytical.

examples.text: The left side of his face drooped slightly, and the doctor noticed the asymmetry at once.
Economists describe an information asymmetry when sellers know far more about a product than buyers.
Researchers found striking asymmetries in how men and women were described in job references.
The architects deliberately used asymmetry to make the new museum feel dynamic and surprising.
I love the asymmetry of this haircut: one side short and the other long.
The tribunal noted the asymmetry of power between a large employer and a single junior worker.

cloze.text: One wing of the butterfly was larger than the other, so its two halves were no longer mirror images: a rare ___ in such a creature.
Economists call it information ___: the seller of a used car knows far more about it than the buyer.
Few faces are perfect mirror images: small ___ between the left and right sides, such as one ear sitting higher, are completely normal.

misuse.text: The two halves of the logo match exactly, giving it a pleasing asymmetry.
misuse.why: Asymmetry means the sides do not match; matching halves show symmetry.

misuse.text: The asymmetry of the room was five metres by four.
misuse.why: Asymmetry is a lack of balance between parts, not a measurement; for size use 'dimensions'.

phrases: There is a clear asymmetry between... and...

synonyms.vs: Imbalance is everyday and often suggests a problem; asymmetry is more neutral and analytical.
Disparity stresses a large or unfair difference, often in wealth or outcomes; asymmetry is about structure or relationship.
Irregularity means not following a pattern; asymmetry specifically means two sides differ.

origin: From Greek asymmetria, 'lack of proportion', from a-, 'not', and symmetria, 'proportion'.

sense: boldly daring, willing to take risks
definition: Very bold and willing to take surprising risks, sometimes in a shocking or disrespectful way.
nuance: Audacious can be admiring, for a daring plan or brilliant move, or critical, for shameless cheek. The context shows which: 'an audacious goal' praises, 'an audacious lie' condemns. It is common in sport, business and reviews.

examples.text: In an audacious move, the goalkeeper ran the length of the pitch and scored in the final minute.
It was an audacious plan: sneak into the castle dressed as the king's own guards.
Historians describe the Apollo programme as an audacious gamble that few experts expected to succeed.
Asking the boss for a pay rise in your first week is pretty audacious, I'll give you that.
The board approved an audacious plan to double the charity's reach within five years.
Darwin's audacious claim that humans share ancestors with apes shocked many Victorian readers.

cloze.text: The young player made an ___ attempt to score from the halfway line, a daring risk that was either brilliant or mad.
It was an ___ lie: in front of the whole class, she claimed she had written the famous poem herself.
In an ___ bid that stunned the industry, the tiny company tried to buy a rival a hundred times its size.

misuse.text: The audacious mouse hid in the corner, too frightened to move.
misuse.why: Audacious means bold and daring, so it clashes with a frightened animal that stays hidden.

misuse.text: The concert was so audacious that we could hear it from the next street.
misuse.why: Audacious means daring, not loud; for loud music use 'deafening' or 'audible'.

synonyms.vs: Bold is general and usually positive; audacious is stronger, suggesting a startling risk.
Daring stresses courage in taking risks; audacious can also suggest cheek or disregard for rules.
Brazen is clearly critical, suggesting shameless behaviour; audacious can be admiring.
Reckless means careless about danger; audacious implies a deliberate, often clever risk.

origin: From Latin audax, 'bold', from audere, 'to dare'.

definition: Not sincere, especially by pretending to know less or be more honest than you really are.
nuance: Disingenuous is a polite but pointed way of accusing someone of insincerity, often in politics, business or debate. It suggests a pretence of innocence or frankness rather than an outright lie. It is the opposite of ingenuous, which means innocent and open.

examples.text: It's a bit disingenuous to say you never saw my message when you liked it straight away.
Critics called the company's apology disingenuous, since it continued the same practice the next day.
The author's claim to be a neutral observer is disingenuous, given his close ties to the campaign.
She gave a disingenuous smile and asked, as if she didn't know, who had broken the vase.
The tribunal found the manager's account of the dismissal disingenuous and at odds with the documents.
Scholars have long debated whether the narrator's confusion is real or disingenuous.

cloze.text: It is ___ to claim you knew nothing about the plan when your name is on every email: you are only pretending to be innocent.
It would be ___ of me to pretend I had never heard of the plan, so let me be frank: I helped to write it.
Calling a huge price rise a 'small adjustment' is ___: it pretends to be frank while hiding the truth.

misuse.text: She was disingenuous and told us everything openly and honestly.
misuse.why: Disingenuous means insincere or falsely innocent, the opposite of open and honest.

misuse.text: The inventor came up with a disingenuous solution that saved the company millions.
misuse.why: Disingenuous means insincere; for a clever solution use 'ingenious'.

phrases: It would be disingenuous to suggest that...

synonyms.vs: Insincere is plain and general; disingenuous suggests a deliberate pretence of innocence or frankness.
Dishonest is broader and blunter; disingenuous is more polite and often about misleading framing rather than lies.
Hypocritical means saying one thing and doing another; disingenuous means pretending to be more naive or honest than you are.

confusables.note: Ingenuous means innocent, trusting and open, the opposite.
Ingenious means clever and inventive.

origin: Formed in English from dis- and ingenuous, 'innocent and frank', which comes from Latin ingenuus, 'freeborn, honest'.

definition: Going far beyond ordinary limits, in excellence or beyond the physical world and everyday experience.
nuance: Transcendent has two linked uses: high praise for something extraordinary, as in 'a transcendent performance', and, in religion and philosophy, something that exists beyond the physical world. It is formal and admiring. Do not confuse it with transcendental, used of particular philosophies and of meditation.

examples.text: Critics called his performance as Hamlet transcendent, far beyond anything he had done before.
Many religions describe a transcendent God who exists beyond space and time.
Honestly, watching the sunrise from the summit was transcendent; I forgot how cold I was.
For a few transcendent minutes, the choir's voices made him forget the war outside.
The prize recognises transcendent achievement in the arts, not merely competent work.
Romantic poets often sought transcendent truths in nature rather than in reason or science.

cloze.text: Many believers describe God as ___: existing beyond the physical world and human understanding.
It was not just a good concert but a ___ one, an experience that seemed to lift the audience out of themselves.
Mystics claim that meditation can bring ___ moments of peace, far beyond ordinary thought and feeling.

misuse.text: The film was transcendent: dull, predictable and instantly forgettable.
misuse.why: Transcendent means extraordinary, so it cannot describe a dull and forgettable film.

misuse.text: Her talent transcendent all her rivals by the age of twelve.
misuse.why: Transcendent is an adjective; the verb needed here is 'transcended'.

synonyms.vs: Sublime stresses awe-inspiring beauty or grandeur; transcendent stresses going beyond normal limits.
Extraordinary is general; transcendent suggests rising above the ordinary to a higher, almost spiritual level.

origin: From Latin transcendere, 'to climb over or beyond', from trans-, 'beyond', and scandere, 'to climb'.

sense: a person who lives alone, avoiding others
definition: A person who lives alone and deliberately avoids other people and social life.
nuance: A recluse chooses to withdraw from society, often for years. The word can be neutral or slightly sad, and is common in stories about writers, artists and the very rich. The adjective reclusive is used even more often.

examples.text: After his wife died, the old farmer became a recluse, rarely leaving his cottage or speaking to anyone.
The novelist, a lifelong recluse, turned down every request for an interview.
Studies of young recluses in Japan suggest that social withdrawal often begins in adolescence.
I'm turning into a recluse; I haven't left the flat all weekend.
Biographers have portrayed the poet as a recluse, though her letters reveal a lively circle of friends.
The estate passed to the town after the death of its owner, a recluse who had received no visitors for thirty years.

cloze.text: Since retiring, the famous actor has become a ___: he never leaves his London house and turns away every visitor.
The billionaire became a ___ in later life, living alone behind locked gates and never appearing in public.
Lockdown turned many sociable people into virtual ___, shut away at home and avoiding all company.

misuse.text: She is a real recluse, always out at parties and meeting new friends.
misuse.why: A recluse avoids company, so someone always at parties is the opposite.

misuse.text: The prisoner lived as a recluse in a locked cell for ten years.
misuse.why: A recluse chooses to live apart; someone locked up against their will is in isolation, not a recluse.

synonyms.vs: A hermit often lives alone for religious reasons or in a remote place; a recluse may simply avoid people at home.
A loner prefers to be alone but may still lead an ordinary social life; a recluse withdraws completely.
An introvert prefers quiet and small groups; it describes personality, not a life cut off from others.

origin: From Old French reclus, 'shut away', from Late Latin recludere, 'to shut away', based on claudere, 'to shut'.

definition: To deliberately avoid using, doing or having something, usually on principle.
nuance: Eschew is a formal, somewhat literary verb for avoiding something as a matter of choice or principle: eschew violence, eschew jargon, eschew luxury. It takes a direct object, so do not add 'from'. It is pronounced es-CHOO.

examples.text: The chef eschews fancy gadgets, cooking everything over an open fire with a single iron pan.
Good academic writing should eschew jargon wherever a plain word will do.
The movement eschewed violence, relying instead on boycotts and peaceful marches.
I've been eschewing social media all month, and I'm sleeping much better.
She eschewed the lift and climbed all twelve floors, determined to arrive before him.
The fund eschews investment in tobacco and gambling companies.

cloze.text: The minimalist designer chose to ___ decoration entirely, avoiding anything that served no purpose.
Monks of the order ___ all luxury on principle: they own nothing and sleep on simple wooden beds.
Many modern novelists have ___ long descriptions, deliberately avoiding them in favour of fast dialogue.

misuse.text: He eschewed from eating meat for a whole year.
misuse.why: Eschew takes a direct object without 'from': 'he eschewed meat'.

misuse.text: We eschewed the train by two minutes and had to wait an hour for the next one.
misuse.why: Eschew means avoid on purpose; for missing a train by accident, say 'missed'.

phrases: The author eschews... in favour of...

synonyms.vs: Avoid is everyday and can be accidental or practical; eschew suggests a deliberate, principled choice.
Shun is stronger and often used for rejecting people; eschew is used more for practices and things.
Abstain means choosing not to do something, often drinking or voting, and takes 'from'; eschew takes a direct object.

origin: From Old French eschiver, 'to avoid or dodge', from a Germanic root.

sense: reject as untrue, invalid or binding
definition: To reject something firmly and publicly, refusing to accept it as true, valid or binding.
nuance: Repudiate is a strong, formal verb for openly rejecting claims, ideas, agreements or debts. People repudiate allegations, and governments repudiate treaties. It is stronger than deny: it suggests casting something off completely.

examples.text: The scientist publicly repudiated the study after discovering that its data had been faked.
In his later work, the philosopher repudiated the views of his youth, calling them naive.
Revolutionary governments have sometimes chosen to repudiate the debts of the regimes they replaced, alarming foreign lenders.
He repudiated everything his wealthy family stood for and moved to a fishing village to paint.
She's basically repudiating everything she said last week, which is a bit awkward.
The company repudiates all allegations of wrongdoing and will cooperate fully with the inquiry.

cloze.text: The new government ___ the old regime's foreign debts, declaring them invalid and refusing to pay back a penny.
The union voted to ___ the agreement, refusing to be bound by terms it had never accepted.
By publicly ___ the extremists, the leader made clear that their views had no place in the group.

misuse.text: The committee repudiated the proposal enthusiastically and put it into action at once.
misuse.why: To repudiate is to reject something firmly, not to accept it.

misuse.text: The teacher repudiated the student for talking in class.
misuse.why: Repudiate means rejecting claims or ties, not telling someone off; use 'reprimanded'.

phrases: This view has since been repudiated by...

synonyms.vs: Reject is general; repudiate is more formal and forceful, and often public.
Deny means saying a claim is untrue; repudiate can also mean refusing to honour or be linked to something.
Disown is mostly about cutting ties with a person; repudiate is more often used for ideas, claims and agreements.
Renounce means formally giving up a right, title or belief; repudiate stresses rejecting something as wrong or invalid.

origin: From Latin repudiare, 'to divorce or reject', from repudium, 'divorce'.

sense: cause a feeling or situation to develop
definition: To cause a feeling, attitude or situation to develop.
nuance: Engender is a formal verb used with abstract results: trust, loyalty, fear, debate, resentment. It suggests gradually producing a feeling or condition rather than causing a single event. It is common in academic and policy writing.

examples.text: The new coach's honesty engendered trust among players who had felt ignored for years.
Unequal pay often engenders resentment and lowers morale across an organisation.
The proposal has engendered considerable debate among members and will be discussed again in May.
Studies suggest that cooperative games engender a sense of belonging in young children.
Cancelling at the last minute isn't exactly engendering goodwill with your friends.
Years of silence had engendered a quiet bitterness between the two brothers.

cloze.text: Secrecy tends to ___ suspicion: when staff are told nothing, mistrust slowly takes root and grows.
The unfair decision ___ a lasting resentment that slowly poisoned the whole office.
Teachers hope that small class projects will ___ a love of science, giving rise to lifelong curiosity.

misuse.text: The new factory engenders three hundred cars a day.
misuse.why: Engender is used for feelings and situations, not manufactured objects; use 'produces'.

misuse.text: Climbing without a rope can seriously engender your life.
misuse.why: Engender means cause or produce; the word for putting your life at risk is 'endanger'.

synonyms.vs: Cause is general and can be sudden; engender suggests gradually bringing a feeling or condition into being.
Foster means deliberately encouraging something good; engender can produce good or bad results.
Breed is less formal and often negative, as in 'breed resentment'; engender is neutral and formal.
Provoke suggests a quick, strong reaction; engender suggests a slower development.

confusables.note: Endanger means put someone or something at risk.

origin: From Old French engendrer, from Latin ingenerare, 'to produce', built on generare, 'to beget'.

sense: a descriptive word or phrase for someone
definition: A word or phrase added to a name to describe a person's character or qualities.
nuance: An epithet can be neutral or admiring, like 'the Great' in Alexander the Great, or 'grey-eyed' for Athena in Homer. In modern usage, especially American, it often means an insulting term for someone. In essays about literature and history, it usually means the descriptive kind.

examples.text: King Richard I earned the epithet 'the Lionheart' for his courage in battle.
Homer uses repeated epithets such as 'swift-footed Achilles' to help listeners follow the story.
The striker's epithet, 'the Machine', reflects how reliably he scores.
Grandma calls me 'the professor', an epithet I earned by correcting everyone at dinner.
The villagers whispered their epithet for her, 'the witch of the hill', whenever she passed.
The exhibition notes explain how Elizabeth I came to be known by her famous epithets, 'the Virgin Queen' and 'Good Queen Bess'.

cloze.text: Alexander earned the ___ 'the Great', a descriptive phrase added to his name after his conquests.
Homer often adds a fixed ___ to a name, such as 'rosy-fingered' Dawn or 'wise' Odysseus.
The press gave him the ___ 'the Iron Chancellor', a label added to his name to describe his tough character.

misuse.text: The epithet on her grave simply read, 'Here lies a beloved teacher.'
misuse.why: Words on a grave are an epitaph; an epithet is a descriptive name or phrase.

misuse.text: The novel ends with a short epithet in which the author thanks her family.
misuse.why: A closing section is an epilogue or acknowledgement; an epithet is a descriptive word or phrase added to a name.

synonyms.vs: A nickname is informal and often affectionate; an epithet is a more formal descriptive phrase, often in history or literature.
A title is an official name of rank or office; an epithet describes character or qualities.
A label is any descriptive term, often a reductive one; epithet is literary and attached to a name.

confusables.note: An epitaph is the words written on a gravestone.
An epigraph is a short quotation at the start of a book or chapter.

origin: From Greek epitheton, 'something added', from epi-, 'on', and tithenai, 'to place'.

sense: swing back and forth between two states
definition: To keep moving or changing back and forth between two positions, states, opinions or feelings.
nuance: Oscillate began as a physics word for regular swinging, as of a pendulum or a wave. In essays it is often used for people, moods, policies or prices that keep shifting between two extremes. It is neutral and slightly formal.

examples.text: A pendulum oscillates, swinging back and forth at a steady rate, which made it ideal for keeping time in early clocks.
Public opinion oscillated between support and suspicion throughout the war.
Fuel prices have oscillated wildly this year, leaving drivers unsure what to expect.
I keep oscillating between wanting a dog and knowing I'd never walk it.
His mood would oscillate between cheerful chatter and sudden, heavy silence.
The report notes that policy tends to oscillate between central control and local freedom.

cloze.text: In strong winds the bridge began to ___, swaying back and forth so violently that it was closed.
Like a pendulum, her mood ___ between excitement and dread all week, never settling on how she felt about the move.
Instead of settling on one view, the essay keeps ___ back and forth between two opposing positions.

misuse.text: The temperature oscillated steadily upwards, rising every single day.
misuse.why: Oscillate means moving back and forth, not rising steadily in one direction.

misuse.text: He oscillated the decision for weeks before finally accepting the job.
misuse.why: Oscillate does not take an object; you oscillate between options, not 'oscillate a decision'.

synonyms.vs: Vacillate is mostly about indecision in people; oscillate can also describe physical movement and prices.
Fluctuate means changing irregularly up and down; oscillate suggests movement between two fairly fixed points.
Waver suggests weakness or doubt over one decision; oscillate suggests repeated swings between two sides.

confusables.note: Osculate is a rare, jokey word meaning to kiss.

origin: From Latin oscillare, 'to swing'.

definition: The use of deliberate, obvious exaggeration for effect, not meant to be taken literally.
nuance: Hyperbole is a common term in literary analysis and media criticism, for exaggeration used to impress, amuse or persuade. 'I've told you a million times' is everyday hyperbole. It has four syllables: hy-PER-bo-lee.

examples.text: Saying the queue was a mile long was hyperbole; there were about twenty people in it.
The poet uses hyperbole, promising to love her until the seas run dry.
Advertisers rely on hyperbole, promising that every new phone will change your life.
It is no hyperbole to say that the new vaccine transformed public health in the region.
'I'm literally starving to death,' he groaned with his usual hyperbole, as dinner arrived.
Political speeches often blend hyperbole with selective statistics to win over voters.

cloze.text: Saying you'll die of embarrassment is ___: you are exaggerating for effect, not stating a fact.
The review's claim that it was 'the greatest film ever made' was pure ___, a deliberate overstatement the critic later admitted was not meant literally.
Writers use ___, such as 'I've told you a thousand times', to stress a point through obvious exaggeration.

misuse.text: The report was full of hyperbole, carefully understating every risk.
misuse.why: Hyperbole is exaggeration, the opposite of understatement.

misuse.text: The spacecraft followed a perfect hyperbole as it swung past Jupiter.
misuse.why: The curve is a hyperbola; hyperbole means exaggeration.

phrases: It is no hyperbole to say that...

synonyms.vs: Exaggeration is everyday and can be accidental or dishonest; hyperbole is deliberate, obvious and for effect.
Overstatement is milder and often unintended; hyperbole is extreme and clearly not literal.
Hype is informal and about promotion and publicity; hyperbole is a figure of speech in any context.

confusables.note: A hyperbola is a type of curve in mathematics.

origin: From Greek hyperbole, 'excess', literally 'a throwing beyond', from hyper-, 'beyond', and ballein, 'to throw'.

sense: calm someone's anger, often with a concession
definition: To make someone less angry or upset, usually by doing or giving them something they want.
nuance: Placate is used when someone calms an angry person or group, often with a concession. It can hint that the gesture is shallow and only meant to keep the peace. It is common in news about politics, business and customers.

examples.text: To placate the furious passengers, the airline offered everyone a free meal and a hotel room.
Historians argue that the king's reforms were designed to placate the nobles rather than help the poor.
I placated my little sister with chocolate after breaking her headphones, and she's finally speaking to me again.
He raised his hands in a placating gesture, but the dog kept growling.
The revised timetable is unlikely to placate residents who objected to the original plan.
